title: Basics of Electricity & Electronics
description: Voltage, current, resistance, circuits, and the fundamental components every hardware engineer needs to know.

lessons.title: Voltage, Current & Resistance
lessons.content:
The three basics

Voltage (V), measured in volts, is the electrical "pressure" that pushes charge through a circuit -- the difference in electric potential between two points.

Current (I), measured in amperes (amps, A), is the rate at which charge flows past a point in a circuit.

Resistance (R), measured in ohms (symbol Ω), is how much a component opposes the flow of current.

The water analogy

  • Voltage is like water pressure in a pipe.
  • Current is like the rate of water flow.
  • Resistance is like the narrowness of the pipe restricting flow.

Ohm's Law

These three quantities are related by Ohm's Law:

V = I × R

Rearranged for the other two unknowns:

I = V / R
R = V / I
Common unit prefixes used with V, I, and R
PrefixSymbolMultiplierExample
kilok×1,0004.7 kΩ
millim×0.001250 mA
microµ×0.00000110 µF (capacitance)

Worked example

A 9 V battery is connected across a 470 Ω resistor. What current flows?

I = V / R = 9 / 470 ≈ 0.019 A = 19 mA

lessons.title: Electric Power & Energy
lessons.content:
Power in a circuit

Electrical power is the rate at which energy is delivered to or drawn from a circuit, measured in watts (W). Since voltage is energy per unit charge and current is charge per unit time, multiplying them gives energy per unit time -- power:

P = V × I

Combining this with Ohm′s Law (V = IR) gives two more useful forms, handy when resistance is known but not both V and I:

P = I²R
P = V²/R

Worked example

A 60 W light bulb is connected to a 120 V supply. How much current does it draw, and what is its resistance?

I = P / V = 60 / 120 = 0.5 A
R = V / I = 120 / 0.5 = 240 Ω

Energy and electricity bills

Power is the rate of energy use; multiplying power by time gives total energy. Utility bills use the kilowatt-hour (kWh) -- the energy used by a 1000 W load running for one hour -- rather than the joule, since it is a more convenient size for household consumption.

Energy (kWh) = Power (kW) × Time (hours)

Example: a 100 W lamp left on for 10 hours uses 0.1 kW × 10 h = 1 kWh.

Efficiency

Real devices convert some input energy into a form other than the intended useful output -- almost always heat. Efficiency is the ratio of useful output power to total input power:

Efficiency (%) = (Useful output power / Input power) × 100
Typical efficiency ranges
DeviceTypical efficiency
Incandescent light bulb≈ 5% (most energy becomes heat, not light)
LED light bulb≈ 80-90%
Switching power supply≈ 85-95%
Linear voltage regulatorCan be well under 50%, depending on the voltage it has to drop

lessons.title: Series & Parallel Circuits
lessons.content:
Series circuits

In a series circuit, components are connected end-to-end so there is only one path for current. The same current flows through every component, while the total voltage splits across them.

R_total = R1 + R2 + R3 + ...

Parallel circuits

In a parallel circuit, components share the same two nodes, so the same voltage appears across every branch, while the total current splits between the branches.

1 / R_total = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3 + ...

For exactly two resistors in parallel, this simplifies to:

R_total = (R1 × R2) / (R1 + R2)
Series vs. parallel at a glance
PropertySeriesParallel
CurrentSame through all componentsSplits between branches
VoltageSplits across componentsSame across all branches
Equivalent resistanceAlways larger than any single resistorAlways smaller than the smallest resistor
If one component fails openWhole circuit stopsOther branches keep working

Worked example

Two 100 Ω resistors in parallel:

R_total = (100 × 100) / (100 + 100) = 50 Ω

lessons.title: Kirchhoff′s Laws
lessons.content:
Kirchhoff′s Current Law (KCL)

KCL states that the total current flowing into any node (junction) must equal the total current flowing out of it -- charge cannot pile up or vanish at a point in a circuit.

Σ I(in) = Σ I(out)

Equivalently, if current flowing into a node is treated as positive and current flowing out as negative, the sum of all currents at a node is zero.

Kirchhoff′s Voltage Law (KVL)

KVL states that the sum of all voltage rises and drops around any closed loop in a circuit must equal zero -- energy gained from sources around a loop must exactly equal energy given up across the loop′s resistances and other elements.

Σ V(rises) = Σ V(drops)

Worked example: a two-resistor loop

A 9 V battery drives two resistors, R1 = 100 Ω and R2 = 200 Ω, in series.

KVL: 9V = I · R1 + I · R2 = I(100 + 200)
I = 9 / 300 = 0.03 A = 30 mA

Voltage across R1: V1 = I × R1 = 0.03 × 100 = 3 V
Voltage across R2: V2 = I × R2 = 0.03 × 200 = 6 V
Check: V1 + V2 = 3 + 6 = 9 V = battery voltage ✓

Why these laws matter

KCL and KVL are the two fundamental rules that every other circuit analysis technique -- series/parallel reduction, voltage/current dividers, Thevenin/Norton equivalents, mesh and nodal analysis -- is ultimately built from. Any circuit, no matter how complex, must satisfy both laws at every node and around every loop.

lessons.title: Circuit Analysis Techniques
lessons.content:
Voltage divider

Two resistors in series split an input voltage in proportion to their resistance -- the larger resistor gets the larger share of the voltage.

Vout = Vin × R2 / (R1 + R2)

Example: Vin = 12 V, R1 = 1 kΩ, R2 = 2 kΩ gives Vout = 12 × 2000/3000 = 8 V.

Voltage dividers are simple, but "loading" (connecting anything else to Vout that draws current) changes the ratio -- they work best when whatever reads Vout draws very little current compared to what flows through R1 and R2.

Current divider

Two resistors in parallel split an input current inversely to their resistance -- the smaller resistor carries the larger share of the current.

I1 = Iin × R2 / (R1 + R2)
I2 = Iin × R1 / (R1 + R2)

Thevenin′s theorem

Any network of resistors and sources, viewed from just two terminals, behaves exactly like one ideal voltage source (V_TH) in series with one resistor (R_TH):

  • V_TH is the open-circuit voltage measured across the two terminals, with nothing else connected.
  • R_TH is the resistance measured across the terminals with all independent sources turned off (voltage sources replaced by short circuits, current sources replaced by open circuits).

Reducing a complicated network to its Thevenin equivalent makes it easy to see how it will respond to whatever load is eventually connected, without re-analyzing the whole original circuit every time the load changes.

Norton′s theorem

Norton′s theorem is the dual of Thevenin′s: the same two-terminal network can equally be modeled as one ideal current source (I_N) in parallel with one resistor (R_N = R_TH).

I_N = V_TH / R_TH

Thevenin and Norton equivalents of the same network are always interchangeable using this relationship.

Superposition

In any linear circuit with multiple independent sources, the voltage or current anywhere in the circuit is the sum of the contributions from each source acting alone, with every other independent source turned off (voltage sources shorted, current sources opened) one at a time.

lessons.title: Capacitors & Capacitance
lessons.content:
What a capacitor does

A capacitor stores electrical energy in an electric field between two conductive plates separated by an insulator (a dielectric). Capacitance C, measured in farads (F), describes how much charge a capacitor stores per volt across it:

C = Q / V

A farad is a very large unit for most electronics -- practical capacitors are usually specified in microfarads (µF), nanofarads (nF), or picofarads (pF).

Capacitors in series and parallel

Capacitor combination rules (the opposite pattern from resistors)
ArrangementFormula
ParallelC_total = C1 + C2 + ...
Series1/C_total = 1/C1 + 1/C2 + ...

Capacitors combine the opposite way resistors do: parallel capacitors add directly (more plate area, more stored charge for the same voltage), while series capacitors combine like parallel resistors.

Charging and discharging: the RC time constant

Charging a capacitor through a resistor does not happen instantly -- the voltage across the capacitor rises (or falls) exponentially, characterized by the time constant τ (tau):

τ = R × C

τ is the time it takes the capacitor voltage to reach about 63% of its final value when charging (or fall to about 37% of its starting value when discharging). After roughly 5τ, a capacitor is considered fully charged or discharged for most practical purposes.

Capacitor voltage during charging (through a resistor from a fixed supply)
Time elapsed% of final voltage reached
1τ≈ 63%
2τ≈ 86%
3τ≈ 95%
5τ≈ 99% (considered "fully charged")

Energy stored in a capacitor

E = ½ C V²

Common uses

Common capacitor applications
ApplicationWhy a capacitor helps
Decoupling / bulk supply filteringSupplies quick bursts of current and smooths voltage dips near a chip
Timing circuitsThe RC time constant sets a predictable delay
Blocking DC / passing ACA charged capacitor blocks steady DC but still lets a changing AC signal through

lessons.title: Inductors & Inductance
lessons.content:
What an inductor does

An inductor stores energy in a magnetic field created by current flowing through a coil of wire. Inductance L, measured in henries (H), describes how strongly a changing current induces an opposing voltage:

V = L × (dI/dt)

In words: the voltage across an inductor is proportional to how fast its current is changing, not to the current itself. An inductor carrying a perfectly steady current (dI/dt = 0) has zero voltage across it, no matter how large that current is.

Inductors in series and parallel

Inductor combination rules (the same pattern as resistors)
ArrangementFormula
SeriesL_total = L1 + L2 + ...
Parallel1/L_total = 1/L1 + 1/L2 + ...

RL circuits and the time constant

Just as an RC circuit has a time constant τ = RC, an RL circuit (a resistor and inductor in series) has:

τ = L / R

Current through an inductor rises (or falls) exponentially toward its final value with this same time constant, following the same 63%/86%/95%/99% pattern as capacitor voltage.

Energy stored in an inductor

E = ½ L I²

An inductor resists sudden current changes

Because V = L(dI/dt), forcing an inductor′s current to change instantly would require infinite voltage -- in practice, an inductor resists sudden current changes, the opposite behavior from a capacitor (which resists sudden voltage changes). This is why abruptly switching off current through an inductor (e.g. a relay coil) can produce a large voltage spike, usually suppressed with a flyback diode.

lessons.title: AC Signals & RMS Values
lessons.content:
AC vs. DC

Direct current (DC) flows in one constant direction, like a battery. Alternating current (AC) periodically reverses direction, most commonly following a sine wave -- the form electricity is generated and distributed in worldwide.

Describing a sine wave

v(t) = V_peak · sin(2πft + φ)
Sine wave parameters
SymbolMeaningUnit
V_peakMaximum instantaneous voltagevolts
fFrequency -- cycles per secondhertz (Hz)
TPeriod -- time for one full cycle, T = 1/fseconds
φPhase -- how far the wave is shifted in time relative to a referencedegrees or radians
Standard mains AC power
RegionFrequencyTypical voltage (RMS)
North America60 Hz120 V
Europe / most of the world50 Hz230 V

RMS: why AC voltage is not quoted as its peak value

Root-mean-square (RMS) voltage is the equivalent DC voltage that would deliver the same average power to a resistive load. For a pure sine wave:

V_RMS = V_peak / √2  ≈ 0.707 × V_peak

"120 V mains" means 120 V RMS -- the actual peak voltage on a North American outlet is about 120 × 1.414 ≈ 170 V.

Average power in an AC resistive circuit

Once RMS values are used, the familiar DC power formulas apply directly:

P_avg = V_RMS × I_RMS = I_RMS² × R = V_RMS² / R

lessons.title: AC Circuit Analysis: Reactance & Impedance
lessons.content:
Why AC needs more than resistance

Capacitors and inductors oppose AC current in a way that depends on frequency, and -- unlike a resistor -- they also shift the timing (phase) between voltage and current. Reactance is the AC equivalent of resistance for these frequency-dependent components, measured in ohms.

Capacitive and inductive reactance

Reactance formulas
ComponentReactanceBehavior as frequency rises
CapacitorX_C = 1 / (2πfC)Reactance falls -- a capacitor increasingly looks like a short circuit at high frequency
InductorX_L = 2πfLReactance rises -- an inductor increasingly looks like an open circuit at high frequency

This opposite frequency behavior is exactly why RC and RL circuits make useful filters, covered later in this course.

Impedance

Impedance Z generalizes resistance to AC circuits by combining resistance and reactance. Because reactance also shifts phase, impedance is naturally described as a complex number, with resistance as the real part and reactance as the imaginary part:

Z = R + jX

For a resistor and capacitor in series: Z = R - jX_C. For a resistor and inductor in series: Z = R + jX_L. Ohm′s Law generalizes directly: V = I × Z, using complex (phasor) values for V, I, and Z.

Series RLC resonance

In a series RLC circuit, X_L and X_C work against each other because of their opposite signs. At one specific frequency, called the resonant frequency, they cancel exactly (X_L = X_C), leaving only R to oppose current -- current is at its maximum at resonance.

f_resonant = 1 / (2π√(LC))

Resonance is the underlying principle behind radio tuning circuits, which use an RLC-like network to select one desired frequency out of many.

lessons.title: Diodes & Transistors
lessons.content:
Diodes

A diode is a two-terminal component that lets current flow easily in one direction (forward bias) and blocks it in the other (reverse bias). A silicon diode typically needs about 0.7 V across it before it conducts; an LED needs roughly 1.8-3.3 V depending on its color.

Diode behavior by bias direction
Bias directionBehavior
Forward biasConducts current once the forward voltage threshold is reached
Reverse biasBlocks current (until its reverse breakdown voltage is exceeded)

Transistors

A transistor is a three-terminal device used as an electronic switch or amplifier. The most common types are the Bipolar Junction Transistor (BJT), with terminals Base, Collector, and Emitter, and the MOSFET, with terminals Gate, Drain, and Source.

BJT operating regions (NPN transistor)
RegionConditionBehavior
CutoffV_BE below ~0.7 VActs like an open switch, no current flows
ActiveV_BE ≈ 0.7 V, V_CE above saturationActs as an amplifier, I_C proportional to I_B
SaturationV_CE very low (~0.2 V)Acts like a closed switch, fully "on"

In digital circuits, transistors are almost always used as switches: fully off (cutoff) represents a logic 0, and fully on (saturation) represents a logic 1. This is the foundation that logic gates are built from.

lessons.title: Power Supplies: Rectifiers & Regulation
lessons.content:
From AC mains to usable DC

Most electronics need a steady DC voltage, but wall power is AC. A power supply converts AC to DC in stages: rectification, filtering, and regulation.

Rectifiers

Half-wave vs. full-wave rectification
TypeDiodes neededOutput
Half-wave1Passes only the positive half of each AC cycle; the negative half is simply blocked, wasting half the input power
Full-wave (bridge)4 (in a bridge arrangement)Flips the negative half of each cycle positive instead of discarding it, so both halves of every cycle contribute to the output

A full-wave bridge rectifier is by far the more common choice in real power supplies, since it uses the input power far more efficiently and produces a smoother, more easily filtered output.

Filtering

A rectifier alone produces a bumpy, pulsing DC output, not a flat one. A large filter capacitor placed across the output smooths this out: it charges toward the peak voltage on each pulse and then discharges slowly through the load between pulses, filling in the gaps. The remaining up-and-down wobble is called ripple, and it shrinks as the filter capacitor gets larger or the load current gets smaller.

Regulation

Even a well-filtered supply still sags under changing load and still has some ripple -- a voltage regulator holds the output at a fixed voltage despite both.

Linear vs. switching regulators
AspectLinear regulatorSwitching regulator
How it worksActs like a variable resistor, dropping the excess voltage as heatRapidly switches a transistor on/off and filters the result with an inductor and capacitor
EfficiencyLower -- wastes power proportional to the voltage it dropsHigher -- typically 85-95%
Noise / complexityVery clean output, simple to useSome switching noise, more complex, but far less wasted heat
Typical useLow-power, noise-sensitive analog circuitsBattery-powered devices, anywhere efficiency matters

lessons.title: Operational Amplifiers
lessons.content:
The ideal op-amp

An operational amplifier ("op-amp") is a high-gain amplifier with two inputs (inverting, marked "-", and non-inverting, marked "+") and one output. Circuit analysis is made simple by two ideal assumptions:

  • The two input terminals draw no current (infinite input impedance).
  • In a stable circuit with feedback, the op-amp drives its output so that the voltage difference between its two inputs is zero (infinite open-loop gain).

Inverting amplifier

Vout = -(Rf / Rin) × Vin

The negative sign means the output is an inverted (flipped) and scaled copy of the input. The gain magnitude is set purely by the ratio of two resistors, Rf and Rin -- not by anything intrinsic to the op-amp itself, which is what makes op-amp circuits so predictable and easy to design.

Non-inverting amplifier

Vout = (1 + Rf / Rin) × Vin

Here the output is in phase with the input, and the gain is always at least 1 (setting Rf = 0 gives a gain of exactly 1 -- a unity-gain buffer).

Comparator

Used without feedback, an op-amp simply drives its output fully to one supply rail or the other, depending on which input is higher -- a comparator, useful for detecting when a signal crosses a threshold.

Op-amp used as a comparator
ConditionOutput
V+ > V-Output swings to the positive supply rail
V+ < V-Output swings to the negative supply rail (or ground)

lessons.title: Passive Filters
lessons.content:
Filtering by frequency

A filter passes some frequencies while attenuating (weakening) others. The simplest filters combine just one resistor and one capacitor.

Low-pass RC filter

Taking the output across the capacitor in a series RC circuit passes low frequencies (where the capacitor′s reactance is large, so little signal is dropped across it) and attenuates high frequencies (where reactance is small, so most of the signal is dropped across the resistor instead).

f_cutoff = 1 / (2πRC)

High-pass RC filter

Taking the output across the resistor instead gives the opposite behavior: high frequencies pass through relatively unattenuated, while low frequencies are blocked (the capacitor′s large reactance at low frequency drops most of the signal there instead).

f_cutoff = 1 / (2πRC)   (same formula, same components, different output node)

The cutoff frequency

At f_cutoff, the output power is reduced to half of its input value (the voltage drops to about 70.7% of the input, or -3 dB) -- this is the conventional dividing line between a filter′s "passband" and its "stopband," even though the roll-off beyond that point is gradual rather than a hard cutoff.

RL filters

Resistor-inductor pairs form filters the same way, just with the roles reversed compared to RC, since inductive reactance rises with frequency instead of falling: a resistor-inductor low-pass filter takes its output across the resistor, and a high-pass filter takes its output across the inductor.

lessons.title: Electromagnetism & Induction
lessons.content:
Current creates a magnetic field

Any current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field around it; coiling the wire concentrates and strengthens that field, which is exactly what an inductor is. Wrapping the coil around an iron core concentrates it further still -- the basis of electromagnets, relays, and motor windings.

Faraday′s law of induction

A changing magnetic field through a coil induces a voltage in that coil, proportional to how fast the magnetic flux is changing:

V_induced = -N × (dΦ/dt)

where N is the number of turns in the coil and Φ is the magnetic flux through it. This is the principle behind generators (a changing magnetic field, produced by moving a magnet or coil, creates electricity) and transformers (a changing current in one coil induces a voltage in a nearby coil).

Transformers

A transformer uses two coils sharing a common magnetic core to step voltage up or down between its primary and secondary windings, with essentially no direct electrical connection between the two sides.

V_secondary / V_primary = N_secondary / N_primary

An ideal transformer conserves power, so as voltage steps up, current steps down by the same ratio (and vice versa) -- it cannot deliver more power out than is put in.

Motors and generators: the same principle, run in opposite directions

A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force -- the basis of every electric motor. Running that same physical arrangement in reverse, mechanically spinning a conductor through a magnetic field, induces a current instead -- the basis of every generator. This connects directly to the Motor Control lesson in the Robotics course: a spinning DC motor is always also acting a little like a generator, producing a "back-EMF" that opposes the current driving it.

lessons.title: Measurement Instruments
lessons.content:
The multimeter

A multimeter is the single most useful tool in electronics, typically able to measure voltage, current, resistance, and continuity.

How to connect a multimeter
MeasurementConnectionCommon mistake
Voltage (V)In parallel across the two points being measuredNone major -- a voltmeter has very high input resistance, so it barely disturbs the circuit
Current (A)In series, breaking the circuit so current flows through the meterLeaving the meter in current mode while measuring voltage can short the circuit through the meter′s very low resistance, often blowing its internal fuse
Resistance (Ω)Across an isolated component, with power removed from the circuitMeasuring resistance in a live, powered circuit gives a wrong reading and can damage the meter

The oscilloscope

An oscilloscope plots voltage on the vertical axis against time on the horizontal axis, which a multimeter cannot show -- it is the tool for seeing waveform shape, frequency, timing relationships between signals, and glitches that a single numeric reading would completely miss.

Key oscilloscope controls
ControlWhat it sets
Volts/divisionVertical scale -- how many volts each grid square represents
Time/divisionHorizontal scale -- how much time each grid square represents
TriggerThe condition (e.g. a rising edge crossing a set voltage) that tells the scope when to start each new sweep, so a repeating waveform appears stable on screen instead of scrolling

lessons.title: Circuit Protection & Safety
lessons.content:
Fuses and circuit breakers

Both protect a circuit from excessive current, which can overheat wires and start fires, by breaking the circuit before that happens.

Fuses vs. circuit breakers
AspectFuseCircuit breaker
How it worksA thin metal element melts and breaks the circuit when current exceeds its ratingA mechanical (or electronic) switch trips open when current exceeds its rating
After trippingMust be replacedCan simply be reset and reused
Typical useIndividual devices and circuit boardsHousehold electrical panels

Grounding

"Ground" (or "earth") is a common reference point that circuit voltages are measured relative to, and, in mains wiring, a dedicated safety conductor. A properly grounded metal appliance chassis gives a fault current (e.g. a wire touching the case) a low-resistance path back to the source, tripping a breaker or fuse quickly instead of leaving the case dangerously energized and waiting for a person to complete the circuit instead.

Electric shock and safe practice

Approximate effects of AC current through the body (illustrative only -- actual thresholds vary by person and current path)
CurrentTypical effect
≈ 1 mAThreshold of perception (a slight tingle)
≈ 10-20 mAPainful shock; muscles may not be able to let go ("let-go threshold")
≈ 100-200 mACan cause ventricular fibrillation and be fatal

A few practical habits matter far more than memorizing thresholds: always assume a circuit is live until it has been verified otherwise with a meter, discharge capacitors before touching a circuit (they can hold a dangerous charge long after power is removed), work with one hand where practical to avoid a current path across the chest, and never work alone on anything connected to mains voltage.

Electrostatic discharge (ESD)

Static electricity built up on a person or surface can silently destroy sensitive semiconductors (especially MOSFETs) with a discharge far too small to feel. Anti-static wrist straps, ESD-safe mats, and grounded soldering equipment are standard precautions when handling bare ICs and other sensitive components.

description: Boolean algebra, logic gates, combinational and sequential circuits, and number systems.

lessons.title: Number Systems
lessons.content:
Why digital systems use binary

Digital circuits represent information using only two voltage levels: "high" and "low", corresponding to the digits 1 and 0. This is called the binary (base-2) number system. Because raw binary is hard for humans to read, engineers also use octal (base-8) and hexadecimal (base-16) as compact shorthand for groups of bits.

Decimal 0-15 across the common number systems

Converting binary to decimal

Each bit represents a power of two. To convert, add up the powers of two where the bit is 1:

1011 = (1 × 2^3) + (0 × 2^2) + (1 × 2^1) + (1 × 2^0)
     = 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11

Converting decimal to binary

Repeatedly divide by 2 and record the remainders from last to first, or subtract the largest power of two that fits until nothing remains.

lessons.title: Binary Arithmetic & Signed Numbers
lessons.content:
Binary addition

Binary addition follows the same place-value rules as decimal addition, but with only two digits. There are four possible single-bit cases:

Single-bit binary addition
ABSumCarry
0000
0110
1010
1101

Multi-bit numbers are added column by column, carrying into the next column just like decimal addition:

  1011   (11)
+ 0110   ( 6)
------
  10001  (17)

Representing negative numbers: complements

Digital systems have no separate minus-sign wire, so negative numbers are encoded using complements.

Complement systems for an n-bit number N
SystemRuleExample (4-bit, N = 0110)
1′s complementFlip every bit0110 → 1001
2′s complementFlip every bit, then add 10110 → 1001 + 1 = 1010

Two′s complement is what almost all real hardware uses, because it has a single representation for zero and turns subtraction into addition.

Two′s complement representation

In an n-bit two′s complement number, the most significant bit (MSB) is a sign bit: 0 means positive, 1 means negative. To negate a number, take its two′s complement.

4-bit two′s complement range
BitsValue
0111+7 (largest positive)
00000
1111-1
1000-8 (largest negative)

An n-bit two′s complement number ranges from -2^(n-1) to +2^(n-1)-1.

Subtraction using two′s complement

A - B is computed as A + (two′s complement of B), discarding any carry out of the MSB:

A = 0110 (6)
B = 0011 (3)
two's complement of B = 1101

  0110
+ 1101
------
 10011  -> discard the leading carry -> 0011 (3) = 6 - 3

Overflow

Overflow occurs when adding two numbers with the same sign produces a result with the opposite sign -- meaning the true result did not fit in the available bits. Hardware detects this by comparing the carry into the sign bit with the carry out of the sign bit: if they differ, overflow occurred.

Binary-coded decimal (BCD)

BCD encodes each decimal digit (0-9) separately in 4 bits, rather than converting the whole number to pure binary. It wastes some bit patterns (1010-1111 are unused) but makes conversion to and from human-readable decimal trivial -- useful for displays and calculators.

BCD examples

Gray code

Gray code orders binary patterns so that only one bit changes between consecutive values, which avoids glitches when a counter or sensor value is read while it is changing. It is widely used in rotary encoders and in Karnaugh map layouts.

lessons.title: Boolean Algebra Basics
lessons.content:
What Boolean algebra is

Boolean algebra is a mathematical system, introduced by George Boole and later applied to switching circuits by Claude Shannon, that works with variables which can only take one of two values: 0 (false) and 1 (true). It gives a formal way to write, manipulate, and simplify the same logic that a truth table or a gate diagram describes.

The three basic operations

Boolean operations and their notations
OperationAlso calledCommon notationsGate equivalent
ComplementNOT, inversionA′, ¬A, an overbar over ANOT gate
Logical productAND, conjunctionA · B, AB, A ∧ BAND gate
Logical sumOR, disjunctionA + B, A ∨ BOR gate

Despite the "+" and "·" symbols borrowed from ordinary algebra, Boolean addition and multiplication do not behave exactly like arithmetic -- most importantly, 1 + 1 = 1, not 2, because the result can only ever be 0 or 1.

Operator precedence

Just like arithmetic, Boolean expressions have an order of operations: complement first, then AND, then OR (parentheses override this order). For example:

F = A + B · C′

is evaluated as A OR (B AND (NOT C)), not (A OR B) AND (NOT C).

Three equivalent descriptions of the same logic

Any Boolean function can be described in three completely equivalent ways -- a truth table, a Boolean expression, and a gate-level logic diagram -- and a good digital designer moves freely between all three.

Example function F = A′B + AB′ (this is exclusive OR)
ABF
000
011
101
110

A literal is a single variable or its complement (e.g. A or A′). A product term (like A′B) is a set of literals ANDed together, and a sum-of-products expression is several product terms ORed together.

lessons.title: Laws of Boolean Algebra
lessons.content:
Why the laws matter

The laws of Boolean algebra let a designer rewrite an expression into an equivalent -- but simpler, or more convenient -- form without building a truth table every time. They are the algebraic toolkit used to minimize a circuit before laying out gates.

Basic identities

Identity, null, idempotent, and complement laws
LawAND formOR form
IdentityA · 1 = AA + 0 = A
Null / DominanceA · 0 = 0A + 1 = 1
IdempotentA · A = AA + A = A
ComplementA · A′ = 0A + A′ = 1

Involution (double complement): (A′)′ = A -- inverting twice returns the original value.

Commutative and associative laws

Commutative and associative laws
LawAND formOR form
CommutativeAB = BAA + B = B + A
Associative(AB)C = A(BC)(A + B) + C = A + (B + C)

Distributive and absorption laws

Distributive and absorption laws
LawStatement
DistributiveA(B + C) = AB + AC
Distributive (dual)A + BC = (A + B)(A + C)
AbsorptionA + AB = A
Absorption (variant)A(A + B) = A
Absorption (variant 2)A + A′B = A + B

Absorption is one of the most useful simplification tools -- it lets you eliminate a redundant term that is already covered by a simpler one.

Consensus (redundancy) theorem

AB + A′C + BC = AB + A′C

The term BC is the "consensus" of AB and A′C (formed by combining the non-complementary variables of two terms that contain a variable and its complement). It is always redundant algebraically and can be dropped -- though, as the timing lesson later in this course shows, that exact redundant term is sometimes deliberately kept in real hardware to prevent a glitch.

De Morgan′s theorems

De Morgan′s theorems
FormStatementIn words
1(A + B)′ = A′ · B′NOT of an OR = AND of the NOTs
2(A · B)′ = A′ + B′NOT of an AND = OR of the NOTs

De Morgan′s theorems are the reason NAND and NOR gates are "universal" -- they let you convert freely between AND/OR/NOT combinations, which is essential for implementing a design using only NAND gates or only NOR gates.

The principle of duality

Every Boolean identity has a "dual," formed by swapping AND ↔ OR and 0 ↔ 1 everywhere. For example, the dual of A + A′B = A + B is A(A′ + B) = AB. This is why the laws above are almost always listed in AND/OR pairs.

Worked simplification example

F = AB + AB′ + A′B
  = A(B + B′) + A′B      (distributive)
  = A · 1 + A′B          (complement law)
  = A + A′B                 (identity law)
  = A + B                     (absorption variant 2)

lessons.title: Logic Gates
lessons.content:
The basic gates

Logic gates are the building blocks of all digital circuits. Each gate takes one or more binary inputs and produces a binary output based on a fixed rule, which we describe with a truth table -- a table listing every possible input combination and its resulting output.

NOT (inverter)

NOT gate: output is the opposite of the input
AOUT = NOT A

ABOUT = A AND B

NAND and NOR are called "universal gates" because either one, alone, can be wired together to build any other gate -- which is why they are so common inside real chips.

Buffers and tri-state buffers

A buffer is a one-input, one-output gate whose truth table is simply OUT = A -- it does not change the logic value at all. Its purpose is entirely practical: it restores signal strength and drive current on a long wire or a wire feeding many other gates (a "high fan-out" wire).

A tri-state buffer adds a third possible output state, high-impedance (Z), controlled by an enable input. When disabled, the output floats and does not affect the wire it is connected to -- essential for building shared buses where several devices take turns driving the same line.

Tri-state buffer

Building any gate from NAND only

A OR BNAND(NAND(A,A), NAND(B,B))

Building any gate from NOR only

This substitution matters in real chip fabrication: NAND and NOR gates built from CMOS transistors are simpler and faster than AND/OR gates (an AND gate is actually a NAND gate followed by an internal inverter), so digital designs are usually mapped internally onto NAND/NOR networks.

Fan-in and multiple-input gates

AND, OR, NAND, NOR, XOR, and XNOR all generalize naturally to more than two inputs -- for example, a 4-input AND gate outputs 1 only when all four inputs are 1. The number of inputs a gate accepts is called its fan-in. XOR and XNOR generalize as odd/even parity functions rather than "exactly one input is 1": a multi-input XOR outputs 1 when an odd number of its inputs are 1.

lessons.title: Canonical Forms: SOP & POS
lessons.content:
Minterms and maxterms

For a function of n variables, a minterm is a product (AND) term that includes every variable exactly once, either true or complemented, so that it equals 1 for exactly one row of the truth table. A maxterm is the dual: a sum (OR) term that includes every variable exactly once, and equals 0 for exactly one row.

Minterms and maxterms for two variables A, B
ABMintermNotationMaxtermNotation
00A′B′m0A + BM0
01A′Bm1A + B′M1
10AB′m2A′ + BM2
11ABm3A′ + B′M3

The minterm/maxterm index is simply the input combination for that row, read as a binary number.

Canonical sum-of-products (SOP)

Any Boolean function can be written as the OR of the minterms for every row where the output is 1. This is the canonical SOP (or "standard SOP") form.

Example function F(A,B,C)
ABCF
0000
0011
0100
0111
1000
1010
1101
1111
 
F(A,B,C) = A′B′C + A′BC + ABC′ + ABC
         = m1 + m3 + m6 + m7
         = Σm(1, 3, 6, 7)

Canonical product-of-sums (POS)

The same function can equally be written as the AND of the maxterms for every row where the output is 0 -- the canonical POS form.

F(A,B,C) = (A + B + C)(A + B′ + C)(A′ + B + C)(A′ + B + C′)
         = M0 · M2 · M4 · M5
         = ∏M(0, 2, 4, 5)

Notice SOP uses the rows where F = 1 and POS uses the rows where F = 0 -- the two forms are complementary views of the exact same truth table.

Converting between SOP and POS

Given the canonical SOP as Σm(...), the maxterm indices for the POS form are simply all the indices not in that list, with De Morgan′s theorem justifying the switch between AND and OR. Canonical forms are rarely the most efficient circuit to actually build -- the next lesson covers how to minimize them.

lessons.title: Karnaugh Maps & Minimization
lessons.content:
Why Karnaugh maps

Algebraic simplification works, but it is easy to miss a possible simplification by hand. A Karnaugh map (K-map) rearranges a truth table into a grid where physically adjacent cells differ by exactly one bit, so the groups you can simplify are visually obvious as rectangular blocks of 1s.

2-variable K-map

        B=0   B=1
A=0      m0    m1
A=1      m2    m3

3-variable K-map

The column headings are ordered in Gray code (00, 01, 11, 10) rather than plain binary, specifically so that adjacent columns -- including the wraparound from the last column back to the first -- differ by only one bit.

          BC=00  BC=01  BC=11  BC=10
A=0        m0     m1     m3     m2
A=1        m4     m5     m7     m6

4-variable K-map

            CD=00  CD=01  CD=11  CD=10
AB=00        m0     m1     m3     m2
AB=01        m4     m5     m7     m6
AB=11        m12    m13    m15    m14
AB=10        m8     m9     m11    m10

Grouping rules

  • Place a 1 in every cell whose minterm belongs to the function.
  • Circle groups of 1s whose size is a power of 2 (1, 2, 4, 8, 16 cells) -- never groups of 3, 5, 6, or 7.
  • Groups may wrap around the top/bottom edges and the left/right edges of the map (the grid behaves like a torus).
  • Make each group as large as possible, and use as few groups as possible while still covering every 1 at least once.
  • Each group becomes one product term in the minimized SOP: any variable that takes both 0 and 1 within the group drops out; any variable that stays constant across the group appears (true if it stayed 1, complemented if it stayed 0).

Worked example (4 variables)

Minimize F(A,B,C,D) = Σm(0, 1, 2, 3, 8, 9, 10, 11) -- that is, F = 1 whenever the pair (A,B) equals 00 or 10, for any C, D.

            CD=00  CD=01  CD=11  CD=10
AB=00         1      1      1      1
AB=01         0      0      0      0
AB=11         0      0      0      0
AB=10         1      1      1      1

Rows AB=00 and AB=10 are both entirely 1, and (thanks to wraparound) they are adjacent to each other, forming one group of 8 cells in which only B stays constant, at 0:

F = B′

Do not care conditions

Some input combinations may never actually occur (e.g. BCD digit codes 1010-1111), or their output may not matter for a given application. These are marked "X" (don′t care) on the map. You are free to treat each X as a 0 or a 1, whichever helps form a larger group -- but you are never required to cover an X.

Beyond four variables

K-maps become hard to draw and read past five or six variables. For larger functions, the tabular Quine-McCluskey method performs the same "combine terms that differ by one bit" process algorithmically (and is the basis of automated logic minimization tools), followed by a prime-implicant selection step that picks the smallest covering set of terms.

lessons.title: Combinational Circuit Design
lessons.content:
What makes a circuit "combinational"

A combinational circuit′s outputs depend only on its current inputs, with no memory of the past. Every circuit covered in the next several lessons -- adders, multiplexers, decoders, comparators -- is combinational; sequential circuits (with memory) are covered later in this course.

The standard design process

  1. Specify the problem in words, then translate it into a truth table listing every input combination and the required output(s).
  2. Derive a Boolean expression for each output, typically starting from the canonical SOP (or POS) form read directly off the truth table.
  3. Minimize the expression algebraically or with a Karnaugh map to reduce the gate count and the number of levels of logic.
  4. Draw the logic diagram, choosing gates that are actually available (e.g. only 2-input gates, or only NAND gates for a particular chip family).
  5. Verify the circuit against the original truth table, by hand or in simulation, before building or fabricating it.

Design trade-offs

Common trade-offs in combinational design
Trade-offWhy it matters
Gate count vs. speedFewer levels of logic between input and output means shorter propagation delay, even at the cost of more gates
Fan-in limitsReal gates only accept a limited number of inputs; a 6-input AND may need to be built from smaller gates
Fan-out limitsA single gate output can only reliably drive a limited number of downstream gate inputs before needing a buffer
ReusabilityBuilding from standard blocks (muxes, decoders, adders) is easier to design, verify, and reuse than one giant minimized expression

Standard combinational building blocks

In practice, digital designers rarely minimize truth tables by hand for anything but small examples -- most real designs are assembled from a toolbox of standard combinational blocks, each covered in its own lesson next:

Standard combinational blocks covered in this course
BlockPurpose
Adder / subtractorBinary arithmetic
Multiplexer / demultiplexerRoute one of several signals; implement any truth table directly
Decoder / encoderConvert between a binary code and a one-of-many activation signal
ComparatorDetermine equality or ordering of two binary numbers
Parity generator/checkerAdd simple error detection to transmitted or stored data

lessons.title: Adders & Subtractors
lessons.content:
Half adder

A half adder adds two single bits, producing a sum and a carry-out, but has no input for a carry from a previous stage.

Half adder
ABSumCout
0000
0110
1010
1101
 
Sum  = A ⊕ B
Cout = A · B

A half adder is just one XOR gate and one AND gate.

Full adder

A full adder also accepts a carry-in, so full adders can be chained together to add numbers of any width.

Full adder
ABCinSumCout
00000
00110
01010
01101
10010
10101
11001
11111
 
Sum  = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cin
Cout = AB + ACin + BCin

A full adder can be built from two half adders: the first adds A and B, the second adds that result to Cin, and the two carry-outs are ORed together.

Ripple-carry adder

Chaining n full adders, with each stage′s Cout feeding the next stage′s Cin, builds an n-bit adder. It is called "ripple carry" because a carry generated at the least significant bit may have to propagate ("ripple") all the way to the most significant bit, making the worst-case delay grow with the number of bits -- the main drawback of this simple design.

Carry-look-ahead adder

A carry-look-ahead adder computes all the carries in parallel ahead of time instead of waiting for them to ripple through, trading extra gates for much lower delay on wide adders. For each bit position i, define:

Pi = Ai ⊕ Bi          (carry "propagate")
Gi = Ai · Bi           (carry "generate")
C(i+1) = Gi + Pi · Ci     (carry out of stage i)

Because each C(i+1) depends only on the original inputs (through the Gi, Pi, and lower carry terms) rather than on a chain of full adders, these expressions can be expanded and computed with only a few levels of logic.

Half subtractor

Half subtractor (computes A - B)
ABDiffBorrow
0000
0111
1010
1100
 
Diff   = A ⊕ B
Borrow = A′ · B

Full subtractor

Like a full adder, a full subtractor accepts a borrow-in (Bin) so subtractors can be chained across multiple bits.

Diff = A ⊕ B ⊕ Bin
Bout = A′B + A′Bin + BBin

Combined adder/subtractor circuit

Rather than building separate adder and subtractor hardware, real ALUs use one ripple-carry adder plus a control line M: each B input is first XORed with M, and M also feeds the first carry-in. When M = 0, B passes through unchanged and the circuit adds; when M = 1, B is bitwise complemented and 1 is added via the carry-in, which is exactly the two′s complement of B -- so the same adder now computes A - B.

BCD adder

Adding two BCD digits with a plain 4-bit binary adder can produce an invalid result (greater than 9) whenever there is a carry, since BCD only uses codes 0000-1001. A BCD adder detects this (a sum greater than 9, or a carry-out having occurred) and corrects it by adding 6 (0110) to force the result back into valid BCD and to generate the correct carry into the next decimal digit.

lessons.title: Multiplexers & Demultiplexers
lessons.content:
Multiplexer (mux)

A multiplexer selects one of several data inputs and routes it to a single output, based on the value of one or more select lines. A mux with n select lines can choose among 2^n data inputs.

2-to-1 multiplexer
SOutput Y
0Y = A
1Y = B
 
Y = S′A + SB

4-to-1 multiplexer

4-to-1 multiplexer
S1S0Output Y
00Y = D0
01Y = D1
10Y = D2
11Y = D3
 
Y = S1′S0′D0 + S1′S0D1 + S1S0′D2 + S1S0D3

Larger muxes are usually built as a tree of smaller ones -- for example, an 8-to-1 mux from two 4-to-1 muxes feeding a 2-to-1 mux.

Multiplexers as universal function generators

Feeding a function′s input variables into the select lines of a mux, and hard-wiring each data input to 0 or 1 according to the truth table, lets a mux directly implement any truth table with no minimization needed at all -- a technique used inside programmable logic devices, covered later in this course.

Demultiplexer (demux)

A demultiplexer is the mirror image of a mux: it routes a single data input to one of several outputs, chosen by the select lines. All non-selected outputs are held at 0.

1-to-4 demultiplexer
S1S0Y0Y1Y2Y3

Common applications

Mux/demux applications

lessons.title: Decoders & Encoders
lessons.content:
Binary decoder

A decoder converts an n-bit binary code into one active output out of 2^n -- exactly one output line is asserted for each unique input combination.

2-to-4 line decoder
A1A0D0D1D2D3
001000
010100
100010
110001
 
D0 = A1′A0′   D1 = A1′A0   D2 = A1A0′   D3 = A1A0

Each output is simply one minterm of the inputs -- a decoder is really just a bank of AND gates, one per possible input combination. Larger decoders (3-to-8, 4-to-16, and so on) follow the same pattern and often add an enable input that gates all outputs at once, letting several decoders be chained to build a bigger one.

Decoders and demultiplexers are the same circuit

Add a single data input D that gates every AND term (so D0 = A1′A0′D, and so on), and a decoder becomes a demultiplexer. Commercial "decoder/demultiplexer" chips are usually sold as one part that can be used either way.

BCD-to-seven-segment decoder

A seven-segment display shows one decimal digit using seven LED segments labeled a-g. A BCD-to-seven-segment decoder converts a 4-bit BCD digit into the pattern of segments needed to display it.

BCD-to-seven-segment decoder (sample rows, 1 = segment on)
DigitBCDabcdefg
000001111110
100010110000
200101101101
810001111111

Each segment (a through g) is its own combinational output, derived and minimized from the truth table the same way any other combinational output would be -- typically treating the six unused BCD codes (1010-1111) as don′t cares.

Encoder

An encoder is the inverse of a decoder: it compresses one active input line, out of 2^n, back down into an n-bit binary code.

4-to-2 line encoder
D0D1D2D3A1A0
100000
010001
001010
000111

A basic encoder like this is only well-defined when exactly one input is active at a time -- if two inputs are 1 simultaneously, the output is ambiguous.

Priority encoder

A priority encoder resolves that ambiguity by defining, for every input combination, which single active input "wins" -- typically the highest-numbered one -- and ignoring the rest.

4-input priority encoder (D3 has highest priority; X = do not care)
D3D2D1D0A1A0V (valid)
0000XX0
0001001
001X011
01XX101
1XXX111

Priority encoders are the core of interrupt controllers (choosing which of several simultaneous interrupt requests to service first) and of keypad scanners.

lessons.title: Comparators & Parity Circuits
lessons.content:
1-bit magnitude comparator

1-bit comparator
ABA>BA=BA<B
00010
01001
10100
11010
 
(A>B) = AB′
(A=B) = AB + A′B′  =  (A XNOR B)
(A<B) = A′B

Multi-bit magnitude comparator

Comparing two n-bit numbers is done from the most significant bit down: the first bit position where A and B differ decides which number is larger, and if every bit position matches, the numbers are equal. Cascadable comparator chips implement this by taking the equality result of the higher-order bits as an enable for comparing the next lower-order bits, letting several comparator chips be chained to compare wider numbers.

Equality alone is often built more simply as a bitwise XNOR of every corresponding bit pair, ANDed together:

(A = B) = (A3 XNOR B3) · (A2 XNOR B2) · (A1 XNOR B1) · (A0 XNOR B0)

Parity generator

Parity adds one extra bit to a group of data bits so that the total number of 1s (including the parity bit) is always even (even parity) or always odd (odd parity). It is the simplest possible error-detecting code.

Even-parity generator for 3 data bits (sample rows)
D2D1D0P (parity bit)
0000
0011
0110
1111
 
P = D2 ⊕ D1 ⊕ D0

An XOR tree naturally computes even parity (the output is 1 when an odd number of inputs are 1, which is exactly the bit needed to make the total even); inverting it with one more XNOR gives odd parity instead.

Parity checker

At the receiving end, a parity checker XORs all the received bits, including the parity bit itself. For even parity, the result should always be 0; a 1 means at least one bit was corrupted in transmission or storage.

Even-parity checker for the transmitted group (D2, D1, D0, P)
D2 ⊕ D1 ⊕ D0 ⊕ PMeaning
0No error detected
1Error detected (an odd number of bits flipped)

Simple parity can only detect an odd number of bit errors -- if exactly two bits flip, the parity still checks out, which is why more robust systems use stronger codes such as checksums, CRCs, or Hamming codes to detect and even correct more error patterns.

lessons.title: Latches & Flip-Flops
lessons.content:
Combinational vs. sequential logic

Combinational logic (like the gates and circuits from the previous lessons) has outputs that depend only on the current inputs. Sequential logic has memory -- its outputs depend on current inputs and on past state. Flip-flops and latches are the basic 1-bit memory elements used to build registers, counters, and state machines.

SR latch

The simplest memory element, built from two cross-coupled NOR gates: each gate′s output feeds back into the other gate′s input. With both S and R held at 0, the feedback loop holds whichever state (Q = 0 or Q = 1) the latch was already in -- that feedback is exactly what gives the circuit memory. S (Set) and R (Reset) control the stored bit Q.

SR latch behavior
SRQ (next)Meaning
00Q (no change)Hold previous value
010Reset
101Set
11invalidNot allowed

Gated D latch

An SR latch is awkward to control directly because S = R = 1 is forbidden. A gated D latch fixes this by combining a single data input D with an enable input EN: whenever EN is 1, Q follows D; whenever EN is 0, Q holds its last value regardless of D. This removes the invalid state entirely and is the basis for how real flip-flops are built internally.

Gated D latch
ENDQ (next)
0XQ (hold)
100
111

Latches vs. flip-flops

A latch is level-triggered: its output can change any time its enable input is active. A flip-flop is edge-triggered: its output only changes at the instant of a clock edge (rising or falling), and is immune to input changes at every other time. Flip-flops are what almost all real synchronous digital systems use, because they let every part of a circuit change state at the same well-defined moment.

Master-slave construction

A common way to build an edge-triggered flip-flop is to chain two gated latches -- a "master" and a "slave" -- driven by opposite phases of the clock. While the clock is low, the master latch captures the input (the slave is frozen); when the clock goes high, the master freezes and the slave copies the master′s value to the output. Because the master and slave are never both open at the same time, the output changes cleanly on one clock edge and cannot race with an input that is changing at the same time.

D flip-flop

The most widely used flip-flop. On every rising clock edge, it simply copies input D to output Q.

D flip-flop behavior (on rising clock edge)
DQ (next)
00
11

JK flip-flop

A more flexible flip-flop that fixes the SR latch′s invalid state by making both inputs high toggle the output.

JK flip-flop behavior (on rising clock edge)
JKQ (next)Meaning
00Q (no change)Hold
010Reset
101Set
11NOT Q (toggle)Toggle

T flip-flop

A "toggle" flip-flop, often built from a JK flip-flop with J and K tied together, commonly used in counters.

T flip-flop behavior (on rising clock edge)
TQ (next)
0Q (no change)
1NOT Q (toggle)

Characteristic equations

Each flip-flop type has a characteristic equation describing its next state Q(next) as a function of its inputs and its current state Q:

Characteristic equations
Flip-flopCharacteristic equation
SRQ(next) = S + R′Q, with the restriction S · R = 0
DQ(next) = D
JKQ(next) = JQ′ + K′Q
TQ(next) = T ⊕ Q

Excitation tables

When designing a sequential circuit, the current state Q and the required next state Q(next) are usually known, and the task is to work out what inputs will produce that transition -- the reverse direction from a characteristic table. An excitation table lists exactly that.

JK flip-flop excitation table
QQ(next)JK
000X
011X
10X1
11X0
D and T flip-flop excitation tables
QQ(next)DT
0000
0111
1001
1110

Excitation tables are the key tool used later in this course to design counters and other state machines from flip-flops.

Asynchronous preset and clear

Most real flip-flop chips add two extra control inputs, Preset (or Set) and Clear (or Reset), which force Q to 1 or 0 immediately, independent of the clock -- used to force a circuit into a known starting state on power-up.

Timing parameters

Key flip-flop timing parameters
ParameterMeaning
Setup time (t_su)How long the input must be stable before the clock edge for it to be reliably captured
Hold time (t_h)How long the input must remain stable after the clock edge
Propagation delay (t_pd / clock-to-Q)How long after the clock edge it takes for Q to reflect the new value

Violating setup or hold time can cause metastability -- the flip-flop output hovers between 0 and 1 for an unpredictable time before settling -- which is why real designs always leave timing margin, verified by static timing analysis, between when data arrives and when the next clock edge samples it.

lessons.title: Registers & Shift Registers
lessons.content:
Registers

A register is simply a group of flip-flops (commonly D flip-flops) sharing a common clock, used to store a multi-bit binary word. A basic parallel-load register loads all its bits simultaneously from a parallel data bus on one clock edge and holds that value until the next load.

Shift registers

A shift register is a chain of flip-flops where each stage′s output feeds the next stage′s input, so that on every clock edge the stored bits all shift one position, and a new bit enters at one end. Shift registers are classified by how data enters and leaves:

Shift register types
TypeData inData outTypical use
SISO (Serial-In, Serial-Out)SerialSerialFixed-length delay line
SIPO (Serial-In, Parallel-Out)SerialParallel (all bits at once)Serial-to-parallel conversion (e.g. receiving UART data)
PISO (Parallel-In, Serial-Out)Parallel (loaded at once)SerialParallel-to-serial conversion (e.g. transmitting UART data)
PIPO (Parallel-In, Parallel-Out)ParallelParallelBehaves as a simple buffer register

Universal shift register

A universal shift register combines all these modes into one chip, using a mode-select input to choose the operation performed on each clock edge.

Universal shift register mode control (typical 2-bit mode select)
S1S0Operation
00Hold (no change)
01Shift right, new bit enters from the left
10Shift left, new bit enters from the right
11Parallel load

Ring counter

A ring counter is a shift register whose serial output is fed straight back into its serial input, so a single 1 (or a short pattern) circulates endlessly. An n-bit ring counter cycles through n unique states.

4-bit ring counter sequence (single 1 circulating)
ClockQ3 Q2 Q1 Q0
01 0 0 0
10 1 0 0
20 0 1 0
30 0 0 1
41 0 0 0 (repeats)

Johnson counter (twisted-ring counter)

A Johnson counter is a ring counter with a twist: the complement of the last stage′s output is fed back to the first stage, instead of the value directly. This doubles the number of unique states to 2n for an n-bit register, at the cost of the sequence being slightly less obviously "one bit at a time."

4-bit Johnson counter sequence
ClockQ3 Q2 Q1 Q0
00 0 0 0
11 0 0 0
21 1 0 0
31 1 1 0
41 1 1 1
50 1 1 1
60 0 1 1
70 0 0 1
80 0 0 0 (repeats)

Ring and Johnson counters are popular for building simple sequencers (e.g. traffic-light controllers, LED chasers) because decoding "which state am I in" needs no extra logic -- the state is the flip-flop outputs.

lessons.title: Counters
lessons.content:
Asynchronous (ripple) counters

A ripple counter chains T flip-flops (or JK flip-flops wired as toggle, with J = K = 1) so that each stage toggles on the clock edge produced by the previous stage′s output, rather than all being driven by the same clock. This is simple to build, but the toggle "ripples" through the stages one at a time, so propagation delay accumulates with every added bit -- limiting how fast a wide ripple counter can run.

3-bit asynchronous up counter sequence (mod-8)
Clock pulsesQ2 Q1 Q0
00 0 0
10 0 1
20 1 0
30 1 1
41 0 0
51 0 1
61 1 0
71 1 1
80 0 0 (repeats)

Synchronous counters

A synchronous counter clocks every flip-flop from the same clock signal at the same time, and uses combinational logic (typically AND gates) to decide which flip-flops should toggle on the next edge, based on the current state. This removes the ripple delay and lets the whole counter change state in about one flip-flop′s worth of delay, regardless of width.

Synchronous 3-bit up counter toggle logic (T flip-flops)
StageToggles when
T0 (LSB)Always (T0 = 1)
T1Q0 = 1
T2Q1 · Q0 = 1

In general, for a synchronous binary up counter, stage n toggles exactly when every less-significant bit is currently 1 -- the same carry pattern as ordinary binary addition of 1.

Up/down counters

An up/down counter adds a direction control input. For an up count, each T input is the AND of all lower bits (as above); for a down count, each T input is instead the AND of the complements of all lower bits. A mux selects which toggle logic is used, based on the direction input.

Designing a mod-N counter

A counter that must count through only N states (rather than a full power of two) is designed with the standard sequential design process from the next lesson: write the state table for the N desired states, use flip-flop excitation tables to work out the required J/K (or D, or T) input equations for each transition, minimize those equations, and add a reset path for any unused states so the counter cannot get stuck outside its intended cycle.

BCD (decade) counter

A decade counter counts 0000 through 1001 (0-9 in BCD) and then resets to 0000 on the next clock, instead of continuing to 1010-1111. It is commonly built either by adding reset-on-1010 detection logic to a 4-bit binary counter, or by designing the toggle equations directly for exactly those 10 states, using the excitation-table method above.

lessons.title: Finite State Machines
lessons.content:
Finite state machines

A finite state machine (FSM) is the general model behind every sequential circuit: a system that is always in exactly one of a finite number of states, and moves between states based on its current state and current inputs, on each clock edge.

Moore vs. Mealy machines

Moore vs. Mealy machines
AspectMoore machineMealy machine
Output depends onCurrent state onlyCurrent state and current input
Output changesOnly on a clock edge, synchronized with the stateCan change as soon as the input changes, between clock edges
State diagram notationOutput labeled inside each state circleOutput labeled on each transition arrow, alongside the input
States neededOften needs more states to separate outputsOften needs fewer states
Timing behaviorGlitch-free, easier to reason aboutCan react one clock cycle sooner, but outputs can glitch

State diagrams and state tables

A state diagram is a graph: circles are states, and arrows are transitions labeled with the input value(s) that cause them (and, for a Mealy machine, the output produced). A state table lists the same information as rows -- current state, input, next state, and output -- and is simply the truth table for a sequential circuit.

Sequential circuit design steps

  1. Draw the state diagram from the word description of the required behavior.
  2. Write the state table from the diagram.
  3. Assign binary codes to each state (state encoding) -- m states require at least ceil(log2 m) flip-flops.
  4. Build the transition table, substituting the binary state codes into the state table.
  5. Derive excitation equations for each flip-flop input, using the flip-flop′s excitation table to work out what input values cause each required state transition.
  6. Minimize each excitation equation (algebraically or with a K-map) and derive the output equation(s).
  7. Draw the final circuit: flip-flops plus the combinational logic that implements the excitation and output equations.

Worked example outline: detecting the sequence "101"

To design a circuit whose output goes to 1 for one clock cycle whenever the last three bits received on a serial input were 1, 0, 1 (with overlapping sequences allowed):

  • Define states for "no useful bits seen yet," "last bit was 1," and "last two bits were 10," and use the output to flag when a third bit of 1 arrives right after state "10."
  • A Moore version needs an extra state whose sole job is to output 1 (since Moore outputs depend only on state), typically 4 states total.
  • A Mealy version can produce the same output on the transition itself without a dedicated state, typically needing only 3 states.
  • From there, the design steps above -- encode the states, build the transition table, derive the flip-flop equations -- apply exactly as with any other sequential circuit.

State minimization

Two states are equivalent if, for every possible input, they produce the same output and transition to equivalent next states. Removing redundant equivalent states (state minimization) reduces the flip-flop count needed to implement a machine without changing its input/output behavior -- important because unnecessary states cost real silicon area and power.

lessons.title: Memory & Programmable Logic
lessons.content:
Read-only memory (ROM)

A ROM stores a fixed table of data as a combinational circuit: internally, it is a full decoder (one AND-gate output, or "word line," per address -- a fixed, unprogrammable array) feeding a programmable OR array that connects each word line to the output bits that should be 1 for that address.

ROM variants
TypeHow it is programmedReprogrammable?
Mask ROMProgrammed into the silicon at the factoryNo
PROMProgrammed once by the user, by blowing internal fusesNo
EPROMProgrammed electrically, erased with UV lightYes (with a UV eraser)
EEPROMProgrammed and erased electrically, byte by byteYes
Flash memoryProgrammed and erased electrically, in blocksYes

Random-access memory (RAM)

SRAM vs. DRAM
AspectSRAM (static RAM)DRAM (dynamic RAM)
Storage elementA latch (typically six transistors)A single capacitor plus one transistor
Needs refreshing?No -- holds data as long as poweredYes -- the capacitor leaks charge and must be periodically rewritten
SpeedFasterSlower
Density / cost per bitLower density, more expensiveHigher density, cheaper
Typical useCPU cachesMain system memory

Both SRAM and DRAM are volatile: unlike ROM, they lose their contents when power is removed.

Programmable logic: PLA and PAL

A PLA (Programmable Logic Array) and a PAL (Programmable Array Logic) both implement arbitrary sum-of-products expressions directly in hardware, without needing to hand-design gate networks, but they differ in how flexible they are:

ROM vs. PLA vs. PAL
DeviceAND arrayOR array
ROMFixed (every possible minterm)Programmable
PLAProgrammableProgrammable
PALProgrammableFixed

A PLA is the most flexible (any product terms, summed in any combination) but also the most expensive to fabricate; a PAL is cheaper and faster because only the AND array needs to be programmable, at the cost of some of that flexibility.

From PALs to FPGAs

Modern designs mostly use FPGAs (Field-Programmable Gate Arrays) instead of PLAs and PALs. An FPGA is built from thousands of small look-up tables (LUTs, each able to implement any small truth table) plus flip-flops and a programmable interconnect fabric, all configured after fabrication -- typically by compiling a Verilog or VHDL design (see the Verilog and VHDL courses) down to a bitstream that programs the LUTs and interconnect.

lessons.title: Timing & Hazards
lessons.content:
Propagation delay

No real gate switches instantly -- there is always some propagation delay (t_pd) between an input changing and the output settling to its new correct value. In a multi-level circuit, delays add up along the longest input-to-output path, called the critical path, which sets the maximum speed the circuit can be clocked at.

Max clock frequency ≈ 1 / (t_pd(critical path) + t_setup)

Setup and hold time revisited

As covered in the latches and flip-flops lesson, every flip-flop needs its input to be stable for a setup time before the clock edge and a hold time after it. If the combinational logic feeding a flip-flop is too slow (a "setup violation") or switches too fast relative to a shared clock (a "hold violation"), the flip-flop can sample the wrong value or become metastable. Static timing analysis tools check every path in a design against these constraints before it is trusted to work in real hardware.

Static hazards (glitches)

A static hazard is a momentary, unwanted glitch on an output that should stay logically constant while a single input changes -- caused by two different paths through the circuit switching at slightly different times because of gate delays.

F = AB + A′C

Hold B = 1 and C = 1, and let A transition from 1 to 0. Algebraically, F = 1 both before (F = AB = 1) and after (F = A′C = 1) the transition -- the output should never change. But the AB term switches off only after A falls and propagates through its AND gate, while the A′C term switches on only after A is inverted and propagates through its own AND gate. For a brief moment, both terms can be 0 at once, and F glitches to 0 even though it should have stayed at 1 the whole time. This is exactly the consensus-term situation from the laws of Boolean algebra: BC is the consensus of AB and A′C, and although the consensus theorem says BC is algebraically redundant (AB + A′C + BC = AB + A′C), adding it back as an extra, "redundant" gate removes the hazard, because BC stays 1 throughout the transition and holds F at 1 while the other two terms switch:

F = AB + A′C + BC   (hazard-free)

Dynamic hazards and races

A dynamic hazard occurs when an output that is supposed to change once (0-to-1 or 1-to-0) instead glitches back and forth several times before settling -- typically caused by more than two paths with different delays feeding the same output. A race condition is the more general problem in asynchronous circuits (with no common clock) where the final settled state actually depends on which of two changing signals happens to arrive first, rather than being uniquely determined by the logic -- one major reason most digital systems are designed to be synchronous, using a single global clock and edge-triggered flip-flops to sidestep this entire class of problem.

title: PCB Design
description: Schematic capture, layout, routing, and manufacturing considerations for printed circuit boards.

lessons.title: PCB Fundamentals
lessons.content:
What a PCB is

A printed circuit board (PCB) is an insulating substrate with layers of conductive copper etched into patterns (traces) that connect components together, replacing the loose wires of a breadboard or point-to-point wiring with a mechanically stable, repeatable, and compact interconnect.

Base materials

Common PCB substrate materials
MaterialNotes
FR4 (glass-reinforced epoxy)The overwhelming default for rigid boards -- good mechanical strength, decent electrical properties, and low cost
Rogers / PTFE-based laminatesUsed for RF and high-speed boards where FR4′s electrical losses become significant at higher frequencies
PolyimideUsed for flexible ("flex") and rigid-flex boards, since it can bend repeatedly without cracking
Aluminum-core (MCPCB)Used where a board needs to conduct heat away efficiently, e.g. high-power LED boards

Copper weight

Copper thickness is specified in ounces per square foot -- the weight of copper that would cover one square foot of board at that thickness. 1 oz (about 35 µm) is the standard default for signal layers; 2 oz or heavier copper is used when traces need to carry more current, since a thicker trace of the same width has lower resistance and can dissipate heat better.

Rigid, flexible, and rigid-flex boards

Board construction types
TypeTypical use
RigidThe vast majority of boards -- fixed shape, mounted in an enclosure
FlexibleBoards that must bend or fold, e.g. connecting two parts of a folding device
Rigid-flexCombines rigid sections (for components) with flexible sections (for connections between them), replacing a rigid board plus a separate cable

Layer count, at a glance

A board′s "layer count" refers to the number of copper layers, not the number of physical sheets of material -- a 4-layer board has four separate copper layers (commonly: top signal, ground plane, power plane, bottom signal) separated and bonded together with insulating material. Layer stack-ups are covered in detail in their own lesson later in this course.

lessons.title: Schematic Capture
lessons.content:
What a schematic is

A schematic is a diagram of a circuit using standardized symbols for components (resistors, capacitors, ICs, connectors) connected by lines called nets. It describes electrical connectivity, not physical layout.

Typical schematic capture workflow

  1. Place component symbols from a library (or create custom symbols for parts that are not in the library).
  2. Wire the symbols together to define nets, and label important nets (e.g. VCC, GND, SDA).
  3. Assign each component a reference designator (e.g. R1, C4, U2) and a footprint that matches its physical package.
  4. Run an Electrical Rule Check (ERC) to catch unconnected pins, conflicting outputs, and missing power connections.
  5. Generate a netlist, which is the file the PCB layout tool uses to know which pads must be connected together.
Common schematic reference designator prefixes
PrefixComponent type
RResistor
CCapacitor
LInductor
U / ICIntegrated circuit
QTransistor
DDiode / LED
J / PConnector

lessons.title: Component Footprints & Packages
lessons.content:
Through-hole vs. surface-mount

Through-hole (THT) vs. surface-mount (SMD)
AspectThrough-hole (THT)Surface-mount (SMD)
MountingLeads pass through drilled holes and are soldered on the opposite sideComponent sits directly on pads on the board surface
Mechanical strengthStronger -- good for connectors and parts under mechanical stressWeaker per joint, but usually fine for most components
Board densityLower -- needs drilled holes and more board areaMuch higher -- enables far smaller boards
AssemblyOften hand-solderable, typically wave soldered in productionReflow soldered in production; fine-pitch parts are difficult to hand-solder

Nearly all modern consumer electronics are SMD-dominant, with THT reserved mainly for connectors, large capacitors, and anything needing extra mechanical strength.

Common SMD passive package sizes

Standard SMD passive (resistor/capacitor) sizes
Package (imperial code)Approx. dimensionsNotes
04021.0 × 0.5 mmVery small, needs fine-pitch assembly capability
06031.6 × 0.8 mmA common default for moderately dense boards
08052.0 × 1.25 mmEasier to hand-solder, common on hobbyist and prototype boards
12063.2 × 1.6 mmLarge enough for higher-power resistors, easy hand assembly

The imperial code gives the package length and width in hundredths of an inch -- an "0603" part is 0.06" × 0.03".

Common IC package types

Common integrated circuit packages
PackagePin styleNotes
DIPThrough-hole, two rowsEasy to hand-solder and prototype with, but bulky -- mostly seen on breadboard-friendly and hobbyist parts today
SOICSurface-mount, two rows, gull-wing leadsA common, still hand-solderable SMD package for simpler ICs
QFP / TQFPSurface-mount, four rows, gull-wing leadsCommon for microcontrollers with many pins; leads are visible and can be hand-soldered with practice
QFNSurface-mount, pads on the underside, no visible leadsSmaller than QFP, but requires reflow soldering and complicates hand rework
BGASurface-mount, solder balls in a grid under the packageHighest pin density, but the joints cannot be visually inspected and reliably require X-ray or a proper reflow process to assemble correctly

Land patterns and footprint accuracy

The "footprint" or "land pattern" is the exact copper pad shape and spacing a component needs on the board. Footprints must match the component′s mechanical datasheet precisely -- a footprint that is even slightly wrong can cause a part to sit crooked, tombstone (stand up on one end) during reflow, or simply not solder reliably at all. Most PCB tools ship standard footprint libraries, but any unusual or new component still needs its footprint checked against the datasheet before committing to a production order.

lessons.title: PCB Layout & Routing
lessons.content:
From schematic to physical board

Layout takes the netlist from schematic capture and turns it into a physical arrangement of copper on a board. Good layout balances electrical performance, manufacturability, and cost.

Placement

  • Group related components together (e.g. decoupling capacitors right next to the IC power pins they support).
  • Keep high-speed or sensitive signal paths short.
  • Leave room for mounting holes, connectors, and mechanical clearance.

Routing

Routing draws the copper traces that implement each net. Trace width matters: wider traces carry more current and have lower resistance.

Rough external-layer trace width vs. current capacity (1 oz copper, ~10°C rise)
Trace widthApprox. current capacity
0.25 mm (10 mil)≈ 0.5 A
0.5 mm (20 mil)≈ 1 A
1.0 mm (40 mil)≈ 2 A

These are rough estimates only -- always check a trace-width calculator against your board's copper weight and required temperature rise.

Layer stack-up

Typical layer stack-ups
LayersTypical use
2-layerSimple, low-speed, low-cost boards
4-layerAdds dedicated ground and power planes for better signal integrity
6+ layerComplex or high-speed boards needing controlled impedance and extra routing room

The next several lessons go much deeper into stack-up construction, design rules, vias, power distribution, grounding, and signal integrity -- the details behind why these placement and routing guidelines work.

lessons.title: Layer Stack-Ups in Depth
lessons.content:
Why layer count matters

Adding layers costs more per board but buys dedicated space for power, ground, and extra routing. This lesson goes further into how a stack-up is actually built and why the layer order matters, not just the layer count.

Core and prepreg

The two building blocks of a multilayer stack-up
MaterialWhat it is
CoreA fully cured, rigid sheet of fiberglass/epoxy with copper foil already bonded to both sides
PrepregA partially cured fiberglass/epoxy sheet, uncured until the whole stack is pressed and baked together, that bonds adjacent cores (and any additional copper layers) into one solid board

A stack-up is built by alternating cores and prepreg layers, then curing the whole sandwich together under heat and pressure -- which is why adding layers is not simply "adding more copper foil" but changing the entire mechanical lay-up of the board.

A typical 4-layer stack-up

Common 4-layer stack-up (top to bottom)
LayerTypical role
Top signal (L1)Component placement and primary routing
Ground plane (L2)Solid reference plane, directly under L1
Power plane (L3)Solid or split power distribution, directly above L4
Bottom signal (L4)Secondary routing, sometimes also used for components

Placing a solid ground plane directly beneath the primary signal layer gives every trace on that layer a short, low-inductance return path immediately below it -- important for both signal integrity and EMI performance, covered in their own lessons later in this course.

Symmetry and warping

A stack-up should be roughly symmetric top-to-bottom in copper coverage and material thickness. An unbalanced stack-up (e.g. much more copper on one side than the other) can cause the board to warp or bow after the heat of manufacturing or soldering, since the two sides of the board cool and shrink at different rates.

Controlled impedance

For high-speed or RF signals, the stack-up (layer spacing, dielectric material, and trace width together) is deliberately designed so specific traces have a controlled, predictable characteristic impedance -- typically 50 Ω single-ended or 90-100 Ω differential for common digital interfaces. Fabricators offer impedance calculators and stack-up guidance for exactly this reason, since getting it wrong causes signal reflections, covered in the Signal Integrity Basics lesson.

lessons.title: Design Rules & DRC
lessons.content:
What design rules are

Design rules are the minimum/maximum dimensions a PCB layout must respect so a specific fabricator can reliably manufacture the board -- trace width, spacing, drill size, and more. Every fabricator publishes a design rule set (sometimes several tiers, cheaper for looser rules, more expensive for tighter ones).

Common design rules

Typical design rule categories
RuleWhat it constrainsWhy it matters
Minimum trace widthNarrowest allowed copper traceTraces thinner than the fabricator can reliably etch may end up too narrow, too resistive, or open entirely
Minimum trace spacing (clearance)Closest allowed distance between copper featuresToo little spacing risks solder bridging or arcing at higher voltages
Minimum annular ringCopper remaining around a drilled holeToo little ring risks the pad breaking away from the hole (a "pad blowout") during drilling or use
Minimum drill sizeSmallest hole diameterVery small drills are fragile and break more often during fabrication, raising cost and defect rates
Solder mask clearanceGap between solder mask and copperToo little clearance can leave mask covering part of a pad, or expose copper it should not

ERC vs. DRC

Electrical Rule Check vs. Design Rule Check
CheckRuns onCatches
ERC (Electrical Rule Check)The schematicUnconnected pins, conflicting outputs driving the same net, missing power connections
