    output             error
);
    assign error = ^received;         // 0 = no error, 1 = error detected
endmodule

lessons.title: Multiplexers & Demultiplexers in Verilog
lessons.content:
Intermediate

2-to-1 and 4-to-1 multiplexers

A small mux is often clearest as a ternary expression; the DLD 4-to-1 mux truth table maps directly onto a case statement once there are more than two choices.

module mux2to1 (
    input  sel,
    input  a,
    input  b,
    output y
);
    assign y = sel ? b : a;
endmodule

module mux4to1 (
    input  [1:0]  sel,
    input  [3:0]  d,
    output reg    y
);
    always @(*) begin
        case (sel)
            2'b00: y = d[0];
            2'b01: y = d[1];
            2'b10: y = d[2];
            2'b11: y = d[3];
        endcase
    end
endmodule

Parameterized N-to-1 multiplexer

A common plain-Verilog pattern packs all the data inputs into one wide bus and uses the select value to slice out the right piece:

module mux_n #(parameter WIDTH = 4, parameter N = 8) (
    input  [$clog2(N)-1:0] sel,
    input  [N*WIDTH-1:0]   data_in,   // N inputs of WIDTH bits, concatenated
    output [WIDTH-1:0]     y
);
    assign y = data_in[sel*WIDTH +: WIDTH];
endmodule

+: is an indexed part-select: data_in[sel*WIDTH +: WIDTH] means "WIDTH bits, starting at bit position sel*WIDTH" -- a variable-position slice that an ordinary [hi:lo] range cannot express, since sel is not a constant.

1-to-4 demultiplexer

module demux1to4 (
    input  [1:0]      sel,
    input             d,
    output reg [3:0]  y
);
    always @(*) begin
        y = 4'b0000;
        y[sel] = d;
    end
endmodule

Initializing y to all zeros before the conditional assignment is a common Verilog idiom: it guarantees every output bit has a defined value in every branch, which avoids accidentally inferring a latch for the bits that are not selected.

lessons.title: Ripple-Carry Adders & a Simple ALU
lessons.content:
Intermediate

Ripple-carry adder from a generate loop

Instantiating N full adders by hand for a wide adder is tedious and error-prone. A generate for loop with a genvar lets Verilog create the instances for you at compile time.

module ripple_adder #(parameter WIDTH = 4) (
    input  [WIDTH-1:0] a,
    input  [WIDTH-1:0] b,
    input              cin,
    output [WIDTH-1:0] sum,
    output             cout
);
    wire [WIDTH:0] carry;
    assign carry[0] = cin;
    assign cout = carry[WIDTH];

    genvar i;
    generate
        for (i = 0; i < WIDTH; i = i + 1) begin : fa_stage
            full_adder fa (
                .a    (a[i]),
                .b    (b[i]),
                .cin  (carry[i]),
                .sum  (sum[i]),
                .cout (carry[i+1])
            );
        end
    endgenerate
endmodule

This is structurally identical to the ripple-carry adder from the Digital Logic Design course: each stage′s carry-out wire feeds the next stage′s carry-in, and the delay still ripples from the least significant bit to the most significant bit.

A simple mode-controlled adder/subtractor

Following the same adder/subtractor trick from the DLD course -- XOR every B bit with a mode line M, and feed M into the carry-in -- turns the same adder into a subtractor:

module addsub #(parameter WIDTH = 4) (
    input  [WIDTH-1:0] a,
    input  [WIDTH-1:0] b,
    input              mode,     // 0 = add, 1 = subtract (a - b)
    output [WIDTH-1:0] result,
    output             cout
);
    wire [WIDTH-1:0] b_xored = b ^ {WIDTH{mode}};

    ripple_adder #(.WIDTH(WIDTH)) core (
        .a    (a),
        .b    (b_xored),
        .cin  (mode),
        .sum  (result),
        .cout (cout)
    );
endmodule

{WIDTH{mode}} is a replication operator: it repeats the single bit mode WIDTH times, producing a bus of all 0s (mode = 0, B passes through unchanged) or all 1s (mode = 1, B is bitwise complemented before adding, matching two′s complement negation).

lessons.title: Latches & Flip-Flop Types in Verilog
lessons.content:
Intermediate

Why you rarely write a latch on purpose

An SR or D latch can be described behaviorally, but most synthesis tools flag inferred latches as a likely bug, since an incompletely specified combinational always block infers one by accident. Real designs almost always use the clocked, edge-triggered styles below instead.

// A gated D latch -- shown for completeness, rarely used directly
module d_latch (
    input  en,
    input  d,
    output reg q
);
    always @(en or d)
        if (en)
            q = d;
        // no else: when en = 0, q intentionally holds its value
        // (this is what makes it a latch, and what a linter will flag)
endmodule

JK flip-flop

The DLD course gives the JK characteristic equation Q(next) = JQ′ + K′Q. Implemented directly:

module jk_flip_flop (
    input  clk,
    input  reset,
    input  j,
    input  k,
    output reg q
);
    always @(posedge clk or posedge reset) begin
        if (reset)
            q <= 1'b0;
        else
            case ({j, k})
                2'b00: q <= q;       // hold
                2'b01: q <= 1'b0;   // reset
                2'b10: q <= 1'b1;   // set
                2'b11: q <= ~q;      // toggle
            endcase
    end
endmodule

T flip-flop

module t_flip_flop (
    input  clk,
    input  reset,
    input  t,
    output reg q
);
    always @(posedge clk or posedge reset) begin
        if (reset)
            q <= 1'b0;
        else if (t)
            q <= ~q;
    end
endmodule

Both flip-flops use the same skeleton as the D flip-flop from the beginner lessons: a clocked always block with non-blocking assignment. Only the equation deciding the next value of q changes -- exactly matching the characteristic-equation table from the Digital Logic Design course.

lessons.title: Registers & Shift Registers in Verilog
lessons.content:
Intermediate

A parallel-load register

module register #(parameter WIDTH = 8) (
    input                   clk,
    input                   load,
    input      [WIDTH-1:0]  d,
    output reg [WIDTH-1:0]  q
);
    always @(posedge clk)
        if (load)
            q <= d;
endmodule

SIPO shift register (serial-in, parallel-out)

module sipo #(parameter WIDTH = 8) (
    input                   clk,
    input                   serial_in,
    output reg [WIDTH-1:0]  q
);
    always @(posedge clk)
        q <= {q[WIDTH-2:0], serial_in};
endmodule

Each clock edge shifts every bit one position left and drops the new serial bit into the bottom -- the concatenation {q[WIDTH-2:0], serial_in} builds exactly that new value in one expression.

Universal shift register

Combining hold, shift-left, shift-right, and parallel load into one module, selected by a 2-bit mode input, matches the universal shift register from the DLD course:

module universal_shift_reg #(parameter WIDTH = 8) (
    input                   clk,
    input      [1:0]        mode,   // 00=hold, 01=shift right, 10=shift left, 11=load
    input                   sin_r,  // serial in for shift-right
    input                   sin_l,  // serial in for shift-left
    input      [WIDTH-1:0]  d,      // parallel load data
    output reg [WIDTH-1:0]  q
);
    always @(posedge clk) begin
        case (mode)
            2'b00: q <= q;
            2'b01: q <= {sin_r, q[WIDTH-1:1]};
            2'b10: q <= {q[WIDTH-2:0], sin_l};
            2'b11: q <= d;
        endcase
    end
endmodule

lessons.title: Counters in Verilog
lessons.content:
Intermediate

Free-running binary up counter

module up_counter #(parameter WIDTH = 4) (
    input                   clk,
    input                   reset,
    output reg [WIDTH-1:0]  count
);
    always @(posedge clk or posedge reset)
        if (reset)
            count <= 0;
        else
            count <= count + 1'b1;
endmodule

This single line, count <= count + 1, is what a synchronous counter′s per-bit toggle logic (from the DLD counters lesson) compiles down to -- the synthesis tool works out the individual AND-gate toggle equations for you.

Up/down counter

module updown_counter #(parameter WIDTH = 4) (
    input                   clk,
    input                   reset,
    input                   up_down,   // 1 = count up, 0 = count down
    output reg [WIDTH-1:0]  count
);
    always @(posedge clk or posedge reset)
        if (reset)
            count <= 0;
        else if (up_down)
            count <= count + 1'b1;
        else
            count <= count - 1'b1;
endmodule

Mod-N (e.g. BCD/decade) counter

module mod_n_counter #(parameter WIDTH = 4, parameter N = 10) (
    input                   clk,
    input                   reset,
    output reg [WIDTH-1:0]  count
);
    always @(posedge clk or posedge reset)
        if (reset)
            count <= 0;
        else if (count == N - 1)
            count <= 0;
        else
            count <= count + 1'b1;
endmodule

Setting N = 10 gives exactly the BCD decade counter from the Digital Logic Design course: it counts 0 through 9 and then wraps back to 0, instead of continuing into the unused 1010-1111 codes.

lessons.title: Carry-Lookahead Adders & Generate Blocks
lessons.content:
Advanced

Computing carries in parallel

The DLD course defines, for each bit position i: Pi = Ai ⊕ Bi (propagate) and Gi = Ai · Bi (generate), with C(i+1) = Gi + Pi · Ci. Verilog can compute every carry from these equations directly, without waiting for a chain of full adders:

module cla_adder #(parameter WIDTH = 4) (
    input  [WIDTH-1:0] a,
    input  [WIDTH-1:0] b,
    input              cin,
    output [WIDTH-1:0] sum,
    output             cout
);
    wire [WIDTH-1:0] p = a ^ b;         // propagate
    wire [WIDTH-1:0] g = a & b;         // generate
    wire [WIDTH:0]   c;

    assign c[0] = cin;

    genvar i;
    generate
        for (i = 0; i < WIDTH; i = i + 1) begin : carry_stage
            assign c[i+1] = g[i] | (p[i] & c[i]);
        end
    endgenerate

    assign sum  = p ^ c[WIDTH-1:0];
    assign cout = c[WIDTH];
endmodule

Because every c[i+1] is an independent assign statement rather than a signal threaded through instantiated full-adder modules, a synthesis tool is free to expand and optimize the whole carry chain into a shallow tree of gates -- which is exactly the "compute carries ahead of time" idea the name describes.

generate blocks beyond adders

The same generate/genvar pattern used here and in the ripple-carry adder lesson scales to building any regular, repeated structure parametrically -- an N-bit ring counter, an array of registers, or a tree of comparators -- without writing out each stage by hand.

lessons.title: Finite State Machines in Verilog
lessons.content:
Advanced

Encoding states

Following the DLD design steps, an FSM in Verilog starts by naming and encoding its states, usually with localparam constants instead of hard-coded numbers scattered through the code:

localparam S_IDLE  = 2'b00;
localparam S_GOT1  = 2'b01;
localparam S_GOT10 = 2'b10;
localparam S_MATCH = 2'b11;

Moore sequence detector for "101"

This is the Moore version outlined in the DLD FSM lesson: it needs a dedicated state (S_MATCH) whose output is 1, since a Moore machine′s output can only depend on the current state.

module seq_detector_101_moore (
    input  clk,
    input  reset,
    input  bit_in,
    output y
);
    localparam S_IDLE  = 2'b00;
    localparam S_GOT1  = 2'b01;
    localparam S_GOT10 = 2'b10;
    localparam S_MATCH = 2'b11;

    reg [1:0] state, next_state;

    // next-state logic (combinational)
    always @(*) begin
        case (state)
            S_IDLE:  next_state = bit_in ? S_GOT1  : S_IDLE;
            S_GOT1:  next_state = bit_in ? S_GOT1  : S_GOT10;
            S_GOT10: next_state = bit_in ? S_MATCH : S_IDLE;
            S_MATCH: next_state = bit_in ? S_GOT1  : S_GOT10;
            default: next_state = S_IDLE;
        endcase
    end

    // state register (sequential)
    always @(posedge clk or posedge reset)
        if (reset)
            state <= S_IDLE;
        else
            state <= next_state;

    // Moore output: depends only on state
    assign y = (state == S_MATCH);
endmodule

This three-block structure -- combinational next-state logic, a clocked state register, and a combinational output equation -- is the standard template for describing any FSM in Verilog, and it maps directly onto the DLD design steps: the case statement in the first block is the state table, and keeping it in its own always @(*) block, separate from the clocked block, keeps the combinational and sequential parts of the design cleanly separated.

Mealy version

A Mealy machine produces its output on the transition, which in Verilog means the output equation reads the current state and the current input, instead of state alone:

assign y = (state == S_GOT10) && bit_in;

With this change, S_MATCH is no longer needed as a separate state at all -- exactly the "typically needing only 3 states" difference the DLD FSM lesson describes between the Moore and Mealy versions of the same detector.

lessons.title: Modeling Memory in Verilog
lessons.content:
Advanced

Modeling a ROM

The DLD memory lesson describes a ROM as a fixed decoder feeding a programmable OR array. In Verilog, the simplest behavioral model of that same idea is just an array of registers, initialized once, and read combinationally by address:

module rom_16x8 (
    input  [3:0] addr,
    output [7:0] data
);
    reg [7:0] mem [0:15];

    initial begin
        mem[0] = 8'h00;
        mem[1] = 8'h01;
        mem[2] = 8'h04;
        // ... remaining entries would be filled in the same way,
        // or loaded from a file with $readmemh in simulation
    end

    assign data = mem[addr];
endmodule

Modeling a RAM

A RAM adds a write port: on a write-enabled clock edge the addressed word is updated, exactly like the SRAM described in the DLD lesson (a latch per storage cell, holding its value until explicitly rewritten).

module ram_16x8 (
    input        clk,
    input        write_enable,
    input  [3:0] addr,
    input  [7:0] data_in,
    output [7:0] data_out
);
    reg [7:0] mem [0:15];

    always @(posedge clk)
        if (write_enable)
            mem[addr] <= data_in;

    assign data_out = mem[addr];   // combinational read
endmodule

This combinational-read, synchronous-write style is the most common simple RAM model. Real on-chip RAM blocks are usually synchronous on both read and write (registering data_out as well) to match how physical memory macros actually behave, and to keep timing predictable.

lessons.title: Testbenches & Verification
lessons.content:
Advanced

Why testbenches

Every circuit in this course, from a half adder to an FSM, needs to be checked against its truth table or state diagram before anyone trusts it in real hardware. A testbench is a separate Verilog module, never synthesized, that instantiates the design and drives it with test inputs in simulation.

A simple testbench for the full adder

module full_adder_tb;
    reg  a, b, cin;
    wire sum, cout;

    full_adder dut (.a(a), .b(b), .cin(cin), .sum(sum), .cout(cout));

    initial begin
        $monitor("t=%0t a=%b b=%b cin=%b -> sum=%b cout=%b", $time, a, b, cin, sum, cout);

        a = 0; b = 0; cin = 0; #10;
        a = 0; b = 1; cin = 0; #10;
        a = 1; b = 1; cin = 0; #10;
        a = 1; b = 1; cin = 1; #10;

        $finish;
    end
endmodule

dut ("device under test") is just a conventional instance name. $monitor prints a new line automatically whenever any of its listed signals changes, so the whole simulation timeline shows up without needing a $display after every input change. #10 advances simulation time by 10 time units, letting the combinational logic settle before the next input change.

Clock generation and a self-checking testbench

Sequential designs additionally need a clock generator, and a well-written testbench compares the design′s output against an expected value automatically instead of requiring a human to read through a log. Rather than hard-coding the exact cycle reset releases on, this testbench captures whatever count value appears right after reset is lifted as its baseline, then checks that every following edge increments from there by exactly one -- a pattern that does not depend on precisely hand-tracking simulation timing:

module up_counter_tb;
    reg clk = 0;
    reg reset = 1;
    wire [3:0] count;

    up_counter #(.WIDTH(4)) dut (.clk(clk), .reset(reset), .count(count));

    always #5 clk = ~clk;   // 10-time-unit clock period

    reg [3:0] expected;
    integer i;

    initial begin
        #12 reset = 0;
        @(posedge clk);
        expected = count;   // capture the count right after reset releases

        for (i = 0; i < 20; i = i + 1) begin
            @(posedge clk);
            expected = expected + 1'b1;
            if (count !== expected)
                $display("MISMATCH at i=%0d: expected %0d, got %0d", i, expected, count);
        end

        $display("Test complete.");
        $finish;
    end
endmodule

Writing testbenches like this for every module in this course -- checking each one against the exact truth table, characteristic equation, or state diagram it was designed from in the Digital Logic Design course -- is one of the most valuable habits for catching bugs before a design ever reaches real hardware.

title: VHDL
description: An alternative hardware description language widely used in FPGA and ASIC design.

lessons.title: Entities & Architectures
lessons.content:
Beginner

Entity: the interface

An entity declares a component's name and its ports (inputs and outputs), similar to a Verilog module's port list.

entity and_gate is
    port (
        a : in  std_logic;
        b : in  std_logic;
        y : out std_logic
    );
end entity and_gate;

Architecture: the behavior

An architecture describes what the entity actually does.

architecture behavior of and_gate is
begin
    y <= a and b;
end architecture behavior;

A single entity can have multiple architectures (for example, one for simulation behavior and one for a gate-level implementation), and you choose which one to use at compile/simulation time.

lessons.title: VHDL Data Types
lessons.content:
Beginner

Why VHDL types matter more than in Verilog

VHDL is strongly typed: unlike Verilog, values of different types cannot be mixed in an expression without an explicit conversion, and the compiler enforces this strictly. This catches more mistakes at compile time, at the cost of more boilerplate than Verilog needs for the same circuit.

std_logic and std_logic_vector

The IEEE std_logic type represents a single bit, but with more possible values than just 0 and 1 -- useful for simulating real hardware behavior such as an undriven or conflicting signal.

Common std_logic values
ValueMeaning
'0', '1'Logic low / logic high
'Z'High impedance (e.g. an undriven tri-state output)
'X'Unknown (e.g. two drivers fighting over the same signal)
'U'Uninitialized (a signal′s value before simulation gives it one)
'-'Don′t care
 
library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;

entity example is
    port (
        a : in  std_logic;
        b : in  std_logic_vector(3 downto 0);
        y : out std_logic
    );
end entity example;

std_logic_vector is a bus of std_logic bits -- std_logic_vector(3 downto 0) is a 4-bit bus, with bit 3 as the most significant bit and bit 0 as the least significant, matching the order most engineers read a binary number in.

The two library packages nearly every VHDL file needs

library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;   -- defines std_logic and std_logic_vector
use ieee.numeric_std.all;      -- defines signed/unsigned and arithmetic on them

signed and unsigned: enabling arithmetic

std_logic_vector alone has no defined arithmetic -- VHDL will not let you add two std_logic_vector signals directly. The unsigned and signed types (from numeric_std) are built on the same bits but carry arithmetic meaning, so + and - work on them directly.

signal a, b, sum : unsigned(3 downto 0);
sum <= a + b;   -- valid: unsigned addition

Converting between the two is explicit and common:

signal data  : std_logic_vector(7 downto 0);
signal value : unsigned(7 downto 0);

value <= unsigned(data);               -- std_logic_vector -> unsigned
data  <= std_logic_vector(value);       -- unsigned -> std_logic_vector

integer and other scalar types

integer is useful for things like loop counters and array indices, but is not synthesizable as an arbitrary-width hardware bus the way std_logic_vector is -- it is a simulation and control-flow type, not a signal type meant to model a physical bus of a specific width.

Constants and generics

constant WIDTH : integer := 8;

entity adder is
    generic (WIDTH : integer := 8);
    port (
        a, b : in  std_logic_vector(WIDTH-1 downto 0);
        sum  : out std_logic_vector(WIDTH-1 downto 0)
    );
end entity adder;

A generic is VHDL′s equivalent of a Verilog module parameter -- a compile-time value that lets the same entity be instantiated at different widths without rewriting it.

lessons.title: Signals & Processes
lessons.content:
Beginner

Signals

A signal represents a wire or piece of state inside an architecture, declared with a type such as std_logic (a single bit) or std_logic_vector (a bus of bits).

Processes

A process block groups sequential statements that execute whenever something in its sensitivity list changes -- most commonly a clock.

architecture behavior of d_flip_flop is
begin
    process (clk, reset)
    begin
        if reset = '1' then
            q <= '0';
        elsif rising_edge(clk) then
            q <= d;
        end if;
    end process;
end architecture behavior;

Signal vs. variable

signal vs. variable
KindUpdate timingScope
signalUpdated at the end of the current simulation cycleVisible across the whole architecture
variableUpdated immediately, in program orderLocal to the process it is declared in

lessons.title: Half & Full Adders in VHDL
lessons.content:
Beginner

Half adder: concurrent (dataflow) style

library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;

entity half_adder is
    port (
        a, b      : in  std_logic;
        sum, cout : out std_logic
    );
end entity half_adder;

architecture dataflow of half_adder is
begin
    sum  <= a xor b;
    cout <= a and b;
end architecture dataflow;

Full adder: concurrent style

entity full_adder is
    port (
        a, b, cin : in  std_logic;
        sum, cout : out std_logic
    );
end entity full_adder;

architecture dataflow of full_adder is
begin
    sum  <= a xor b xor cin;
    cout <= (a and b) or (a and cin) or (b and cin);
end architecture dataflow;

Full adder: structural style, built from two half adders

Just like Verilog, VHDL lets an architecture be built purely by wiring up instances of other entities -- exactly matching the DLD lesson describing a full adder built from two half adders.

architecture structural of full_adder is
    signal s1, c1, c2 : std_logic;
begin
    ha1 : entity work.half_adder
        port map (a => a, b => b, sum => s1, cout => c1);

    ha2 : entity work.half_adder
        port map (a => s1, b => cin, sum => sum, cout => c2);

    cout <= c1 or c2;
end architecture structural;

port map (port_name => signal, ...) is VHDL′s named port connection -- the VHDL equivalent of the .port_name(signal) syntax from the Verilog course, connecting each entity port to a specific signal regardless of declaration order.

lessons.title: Decoders & Encoders in VHDL
lessons.content:
Beginner

2-to-4 decoder: concurrent style

entity decoder_2to4 is
    port (
        a : in  std_logic_vector(1 downto 0);
        d : out std_logic_vector(3 downto 0)
    );
end entity decoder_2to4;

architecture dataflow of decoder_2to4 is
begin
    d(0) <= (not a(1)) and (not a(0));
    d(1) <= (not a(1)) and a(0);
    d(2) <= a(1) and (not a(0));
    d(3) <= a(1) and a(0);
end architecture dataflow;

A cleaner decoder using a process and a case statement

architecture behavioral of decoder_2to4 is
begin
    process(a)
    begin
        case a is
            when "00"   => d <= "0001";
            when "01"   => d <= "0010";
            when "10"   => d <= "0100";
            when "11"   => d <= "1000";
            when others => d <= "0000";
        end case;
    end process;
end architecture behavioral;

A process with every signal it reads listed in its sensitivity list (here, just a) is VHDL′s way of describing combinational logic with a case or if statement, matching the role of Verilog′s always @(*) block. The when others branch is required by VHDL whenever a case does not explicitly cover every possible value of its type -- for a 2-bit std_logic_vector, that technically includes values like "ZZ" or "XX", not just the four binary combinations.

4-to-2 encoder

entity encoder_4to2 is
    port (
        d : in  std_logic_vector(3 downto 0);
        a : out std_logic_vector(1 downto 0)
    );
end entity encoder_4to2;

architecture behavioral of encoder_4to2 is
begin
    process(d)
    begin
        case d is
            when "0001" => a <= "00";
            when "0010" => a <= "01";
            when "0100" => a <= "10";
            when "1000" => a <= "11";
            when others => a <= "00";
        end case;
    end process;
end architecture behavioral;

As with the Verilog version of this circuit, the when others branch matters: without it, an unexpected input pattern would leave a holding its previous value rather than a defined one, which can synthesize into an unintended latch.

lessons.title: Comparators & Parity Circuits in VHDL
lessons.content:
Beginner

Multi-bit comparators

library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
use ieee.numeric_std.all;

entity comparator is
    generic (WIDTH : integer := 4);
    port (
        a, b       : in  std_logic_vector(WIDTH-1 downto 0);
        gt, eq, lt : out std_logic
    );
end entity comparator;

architecture dataflow of comparator is
begin
    gt <= '1' when unsigned(a) > unsigned(b) else '0';
    eq <= '1' when unsigned(a) = unsigned(b) else '0';
    lt <= '1' when unsigned(a) < unsigned(b) else '0';
end architecture dataflow;

The when ... else construct is a concurrent conditional assignment -- VHDL′s way of writing a one-line combinational condition without needing a full process block. Comparing as unsigned rather than directly on std_logic_vector is what gives > and < their expected numeric meaning rather than a simple bit-pattern comparison.

Parity generator and checker

VHDL does not have a built-in reduction-XOR operator the way Verilog does, but a small loop with a variable produces the same result.

entity parity_gen is
    generic (WIDTH : integer := 8);
    port (
        data            : in  std_logic_vector(WIDTH-1 downto 0);
        even_parity_bit : out std_logic
    );
end entity parity_gen;

architecture behavioral of parity_gen is
begin
    process(data)
        variable p : std_logic;
    begin
        p := '0';
        for i in data'range loop
            p := p xor data(i);
        end loop;
        even_parity_bit <= p;
    end process;
end architecture behavioral;

A variable (declared inside the process, updated immediately in program order) is the natural tool here, since each loop iteration needs to see the previous iteration′s updated value right away -- unlike a signal, whose new value would not be visible until the next time the process runs.

lessons.title: Multiplexers & Demultiplexers in VHDL
lessons.content:
Intermediate

2-to-1 multiplexer: conditional signal assignment

entity mux2to1 is
    port (
        sel  : in  std_logic;
        a, b : in  std_logic;
        y    : out std_logic
    );
end entity mux2to1;

architecture dataflow of mux2to1 is
begin
    y <= b when sel = '1' else a;
end architecture dataflow;

4-to-1 multiplexer: selected signal assignment

entity mux4to1 is
    port (
        sel : in  std_logic_vector(1 downto 0);
        d   : in  std_logic_vector(3 downto 0);
        y   : out std_logic
    );
end entity mux4to1;

architecture dataflow of mux4to1 is
begin
    with sel select
        y <= d(0) when "00",
             d(1) when "01",
             d(2) when "10",
             d(3) when "11",
             '0' when others;
end architecture dataflow;

with ... select is VHDL′s selected signal assignment -- functionally similar to a case statement inside a process, but written as a single concurrent statement instead. As with any case-like construct over a std_logic_vector, a final when others branch is required to cover every possible value of the selector, not just the two "real" bit patterns.

1-to-4 demultiplexer

entity demux1to4 is
    port (
        sel : in  std_logic_vector(1 downto 0);
        d   : in  std_logic;
        y   : out std_logic_vector(3 downto 0)
    );
end entity demux1to4;

architecture behavioral of demux1to4 is
begin
    process(sel, d)
    begin
        y <= "0000";
        case sel is
            when "00"   => y(0) <= d;
            when "01"   => y(1) <= d;
            when "10"   => y(2) <= d;
            when "11"   => y(3) <= d;
            when others => null;
        end case;
    end process;
end architecture behavioral;

Assigning y <= "0000" first, then overriding a single bit inside the case, is the same idiom used in the Verilog course′s demux example: it guarantees every output bit has a defined value on every path through the process, avoiding an inferred latch on the non-selected bits. null is VHDL′s explicit "do nothing" statement, needed here because the when others branch has no work left to do once the default assignment above has already run.

lessons.title: Ripple-Carry Adders & a Simple ALU in VHDL
lessons.content:
Intermediate

Ripple-carry adder from a generate statement

library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;

entity ripple_adder is
    generic (WIDTH : integer := 4);
    port (
        a, b : in  std_logic_vector(WIDTH-1 downto 0);
        cin  : in  std_logic;
        sum  : out std_logic_vector(WIDTH-1 downto 0);
        cout : out std_logic
    );
end entity ripple_adder;

architecture structural of ripple_adder is
    signal carry : std_logic_vector(WIDTH downto 0);
begin
    carry(0) <= cin;
    cout <= carry(WIDTH);

    fa_stage: for i in 0 to WIDTH-1 generate
        fa : entity work.full_adder
            port map (
                a    => a(i),
                b    => b(i),
                cin  => carry(i),
                sum  => sum(i),
                cout => carry(i+1)
            );
    end generate fa_stage;
end architecture structural;

A for ... generate statement is VHDL′s equivalent of Verilog′s generate for loop with a genvar -- it creates WIDTH copies of the full_adder instance at compile time, each wired to a different bit of a, b, and the carry chain, exactly matching the ripple-carry adder from the Digital Logic Design course.

A mode-controlled adder/subtractor

use ieee.numeric_std.all;

entity addsub is
    generic (WIDTH : integer := 4);
    port (
        a, b   : in  std_logic_vector(WIDTH-1 downto 0);
        mode   : in  std_logic;   -- '0' = add, '1' = subtract (a - b)
        result : out std_logic_vector(WIDTH-1 downto 0);
        cout   : out std_logic
    );
end entity addsub;

architecture structural of addsub is
    signal b_xored : std_logic_vector(WIDTH-1 downto 0);
begin
    b_xored <= b xor (WIDTH-1 downto 0 => mode);

    core : entity work.ripple_adder
        generic map (WIDTH => WIDTH)
        port map (a => a, b => b_xored, cin => mode, sum => result, cout => cout);
end architecture structural;

(WIDTH-1 downto 0 => mode) is a VHDL aggregate: it builds a WIDTH-bit value where every bit equals mode -- the VHDL equivalent of Verilog′s {WIDTH{mode}} replication operator. XORing b against all 0s leaves it unchanged (addition); XORing against all 1s complements every bit, and combined with cin = mode = '1' adding 1, this produces the two′s complement of b -- the same adder/subtractor trick from the Digital Logic Design course.

lessons.title: Latches & Flip-Flop Types in VHDL
lessons.content:
Intermediate

Why you rarely write a latch on purpose

Just as in Verilog, an incompletely specified combinational process in VHDL -- one that does not assign an output on every possible path -- infers a latch rather than combinational logic, which most synthesis tools flag as a likely bug. Real designs almost always use the clocked, edge-triggered styles below instead.

D flip-flop

library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;

entity d_flip_flop is
    port (
        clk, reset : in  std_logic;
        d          : in  std_logic;
        q          : out std_logic
    );
end entity d_flip_flop;

architecture behavioral of d_flip_flop is
begin
    process(clk, reset)
    begin
        if reset = '1' then
            q <= '0';
        elsif rising_edge(clk) then
            q <= d;
        end if;
    end process;
end architecture behavioral;

rising_edge(clk) is the standard, preferred way to detect a clock edge in modern VHDL -- clearer than the older clk'event and clk = '1' idiom still seen in legacy code, though both mean the same thing.

JK flip-flop

entity jk_flip_flop is
    port (
        clk, reset : in  std_logic;
        j, k       : in  std_logic;
        q          : out std_logic
    );
end entity jk_flip_flop;

architecture behavioral of jk_flip_flop is
    signal q_internal : std_logic := '0';
begin
    process(clk, reset)
    begin
        if reset = '1' then
            q_internal <= '0';
        elsif rising_edge(clk) then
            case (j & k) is
                when "00"   => q_internal <= q_internal;       -- hold
                when "01"   => q_internal <= '0';               -- reset
                when "10"   => q_internal <= '1';               -- set
                when "11"   => q_internal <= not q_internal;     -- toggle
                when others => q_internal <= 'X';
            end case;
        end if;
    end process;

    q <= q_internal;
end architecture behavioral;

An internal signal (q_internal) is used here because an entity′s out port cannot always be read back inside its own architecture -- a common pattern whenever a flip-flop′s current output needs to feed back into its own next-state logic, as the toggle case does here. j & k concatenates the two single-bit inputs into a 2-bit vector so they can be matched together in one case statement.

T flip-flop

entity t_flip_flop is
    port (
        clk, reset : in  std_logic;
        t          : in  std_logic;
        q          : out std_logic
    );
end entity t_flip_flop;

architecture behavioral of t_flip_flop is
    signal q_internal : std_logic := '0';
begin
    process(clk, reset)
    begin
        if reset = '1' then
            q_internal <= '0';
        elsif rising_edge(clk) then
            if t = '1' then
                q_internal <= not q_internal;
            end if;
        end if;
    end process;

    q <= q_internal;
end architecture behavioral;

Notice all three flip-flops share the same skeleton: a process sensitive to clk and reset, an asynchronous reset branch, and an elsif rising_edge(clk) branch containing the actual next-state logic -- exactly matching the characteristic-equation table from the Digital Logic Design course, just written in VHDL′s process style instead of Verilog′s always block.

lessons.title: Registers & Shift Registers in VHDL
lessons.content:
Intermediate

A parallel-load register

library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;

entity register_n is
    generic (WIDTH : integer := 8);
    port (
        clk, load : in  std_logic;
        d         : in  std_logic_vector(WIDTH-1 downto 0);
        q         : out std_logic_vector(WIDTH-1 downto 0)
    );
end entity register_n;

architecture behavioral of register_n is
begin
    process(clk)
    begin
        if rising_edge(clk) then
            if load = '1' then
                q <= d;
            end if;
        end if;
    end process;
end architecture behavioral;

SIPO shift register (serial-in, parallel-out)

entity sipo is
    generic (WIDTH : integer := 8);
    port (
        clk       : in  std_logic;
        serial_in : in  std_logic;
        q         : out std_logic_vector(WIDTH-1 downto 0)
    );
end entity sipo;

architecture behavioral of sipo is
    signal shift_reg : std_logic_vector(WIDTH-1 downto 0) := (others => '0');
begin
    process(clk)
    begin
        if rising_edge(clk) then
            shift_reg <= shift_reg(WIDTH-2 downto 0) & serial_in;
        end if;
    end process;

    q <= shift_reg;
end architecture behavioral;

The concatenation shift_reg(WIDTH-2 downto 0) & serial_in builds the new shifted value in one expression -- the VHDL equivalent of Verilog′s {q[WIDTH-2:0], serial_in}.

Universal shift register

entity universal_shift_reg is
    generic (WIDTH : integer := 8);
    port (
        clk          : in  std_logic;
        mode         : in  std_logic_vector(1 downto 0);  -- 00=hold,01=shift right,10=shift left,11=load
        sin_r, sin_l : in  std_logic;
        d            : in  std_logic_vector(WIDTH-1 downto 0);
        q            : out std_logic_vector(WIDTH-1 downto 0)
    );
end entity universal_shift_reg;

architecture behavioral of universal_shift_reg is
    signal shift_reg : std_logic_vector(WIDTH-1 downto 0) := (others => '0');
begin
    process(clk)
    begin
        if rising_edge(clk) then
            case mode is
                when "00"   => shift_reg <= shift_reg;
                when "01"   => shift_reg <= sin_r & shift_reg(WIDTH-1 downto 1);
                when "10"   => shift_reg <= shift_reg(WIDTH-2 downto 0) & sin_l;
                when "11"   => shift_reg <= d;
                when others => shift_reg <= (others => 'X');
            end case;
        end if;
    end process;

    q <= shift_reg;
end architecture behavioral;

lessons.title: Counters in VHDL
lessons.content:
Intermediate

Free-running binary up counter

library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
use ieee.numeric_std.all;

entity up_counter is
    generic (WIDTH : integer := 4);
    port (
        clk, reset : in  std_logic;
        count      : out std_logic_vector(WIDTH-1 downto 0)
    );
end entity up_counter;

architecture behavioral of up_counter is
    signal count_internal : unsigned(WIDTH-1 downto 0) := (others => '0');
begin
    process(clk, reset)
    begin
        if reset = '1' then
            count_internal <= (others => '0');
        elsif rising_edge(clk) then
            count_internal <= count_internal + 1;
        end if;
    end process;

    count <= std_logic_vector(count_internal);
end architecture behavioral;

Counting is done on an internal unsigned signal (since + is only defined for numeric types, not directly on std_logic_vector), then converted back to std_logic_vector for the output port -- the same conversion pattern introduced in the VHDL Data Types lesson.

Up/down counter

entity updown_counter is
    generic (WIDTH : integer := 4);
    port (
        clk, reset : in  std_logic;
        up_down    : in  std_logic;   -- '1' = up, '0' = down
        count      : out std_logic_vector(WIDTH-1 downto 0)
    );
end entity updown_counter;

architecture behavioral of updown_counter is
    signal count_internal : unsigned(WIDTH-1 downto 0) := (others => '0');
begin
    process(clk, reset)
    begin
        if reset = '1' then
            count_internal <= (others => '0');
        elsif rising_edge(clk) then
            if up_down = '1' then
                count_internal <= count_internal + 1;
            else
                count_internal <= count_internal - 1;
            end if;
        end if;
    end process;

    count <= std_logic_vector(count_internal);
end architecture behavioral;

Mod-N (e.g. BCD/decade) counter

entity mod_n_counter is
    generic (WIDTH : integer := 4; N : integer := 10);
    port (
        clk, reset : in  std_logic;
        count      : out std_logic_vector(WIDTH-1 downto 0)
    );
end entity mod_n_counter;

architecture behavioral of mod_n_counter is
    signal count_internal : unsigned(WIDTH-1 downto 0) := (others => '0');
begin
    process(clk, reset)
    begin
        if reset = '1' then
            count_internal <= (others => '0');
        elsif rising_edge(clk) then
            if count_internal = N - 1 then
                count_internal <= (others => '0');
            else
                count_internal <= count_internal + 1;
            end if;
        end if;
    end process;

    count <= std_logic_vector(count_internal);
end architecture behavioral;

Setting the N generic to 10 gives the same BCD decade counter from the Digital Logic Design course: it counts 0 through 9 and then wraps back to 0.

lessons.title: Carry-Lookahead Adders & Generate Statements in VHDL
lessons.content:
Advanced

Computing carries in parallel

library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;

entity cla_adder is
    generic (WIDTH : integer := 4);
    port (
        a, b : in  std_logic_vector(WIDTH-1 downto 0);
        cin  : in  std_logic;
        sum  : out std_logic_vector(WIDTH-1 downto 0);
        cout : out std_logic
    );
end entity cla_adder;

architecture structural of cla_adder is
    signal p, g : std_logic_vector(WIDTH-1 downto 0);
    signal c    : std_logic_vector(WIDTH downto 0);
begin
    p <= a xor b;   -- propagate
    g <= a and b;   -- generate

    c(0) <= cin;

    carry_stage: for i in 0 to WIDTH-1 generate
        c(i+1) <= g(i) or (p(i) and c(i));
    end generate carry_stage;

    sum  <= p xor c(WIDTH-1 downto 0);
    cout <= c(WIDTH);
end architecture structural;

Because every c(i+1) is an independent concurrent signal assignment inside the generate statement, rather than a signal threaded through instantiated full-adder entities, a synthesis tool is free to expand and optimize the whole carry chain into a shallow tree of gates -- the same idea as the carry-lookahead adder from the Digital Logic Design course, and the same trade-off (more gates, much less delay) shown in its Verilog implementation.

generate statements beyond adders

The same for ... generate pattern used here and in the Ripple-Carry Adders lesson scales to building any regular, repeated structure parametrically -- an N-bit ring counter, an array of registers, or a tree of comparators -- without writing out each stage by hand. VHDL also supports if ... generate, which conditionally includes or excludes a block of the architecture at compile time based on a generic value, useful for optional debug logic or alternate implementations selected by a generic.

lessons.title: Finite State Machines in VHDL
lessons.content:
Advanced

Encoding states with an enumerated type

Rather than hard-coding state values as bit patterns, VHDL lets you define a dedicated enumerated type listing the state names directly -- the compiler (and the synthesis tool) chooses the actual bit encoding, which is both clearer to read and less error-prone than managing the encoding by hand.

type state_type is (S_IDLE, S_GOT1, S_GOT10, S_MATCH);
signal state, next_state : state_type;

Moore sequence detector for "101"

This is the same Moore-machine sequence detector introduced in the Digital Logic Design and Verilog courses, following the identical three-part structure: combinational next-state logic, a clocked state register, and a combinational output equation.

library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;

entity seq_detector_101_moore is
    port (
        clk, reset : in  std_logic;
        bit_in     : in  std_logic;
        y          : out std_logic
    );
end entity seq_detector_101_moore;

architecture behavioral of seq_detector_101_moore is
    type state_type is (S_IDLE, S_GOT1, S_GOT10, S_MATCH);
    signal state, next_state : state_type;
begin
    -- next-state logic (combinational)
    process(state, bit_in)
    begin
        case state is
            when S_IDLE =>
                if bit_in = '1' then next_state <= S_GOT1; else next_state <= S_IDLE; end if;
            when S_GOT1 =>
                if bit_in = '1' then next_state <= S_GOT1; else next_state <= S_GOT10; end if;
            when S_GOT10 =>
                if bit_in = '1' then next_state <= S_MATCH; else next_state <= S_IDLE; end if;
            when S_MATCH =>
                if bit_in = '1' then next_state <= S_GOT1; else next_state <= S_GOT10; end if;
        end case;
    end process;

    -- state register (sequential)
    process(clk, reset)
    begin
        if reset = '1' then
            state <= S_IDLE;
        elsif rising_edge(clk) then
            state <= next_state;
        end if;
    end process;

    -- Moore output: depends only on state
    y <= '1' when state = S_MATCH else '0';
end architecture behavioral;

Because state_type is an enumeration with exactly four possible values, the case statement above already covers every case -- unlike the std_logic_vector-based examples earlier in this course, no when others branch is needed here.

Mealy version

A Mealy machine produces its output on the transition, which in VHDL means the output equation reads the current state and the current input, instead of state alone:

y <= '1' when (state = S_GOT10 and bit_in = '1') else '0';

With this change, S_MATCH is no longer needed as a separate state at all -- exactly the same Moore-vs-Mealy trade-off the Digital Logic Design and Verilog courses describe for this same detector.

lessons.title: Modeling Memory in VHDL
lessons.content:
Advanced

Modeling a ROM

VHDL models memory as an array type -- a signal (or constant) whose elements are themselves vectors, indexed like a small lookup table.

library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
use ieee.numeric_std.all;

entity rom_16x8 is
    port (
        addr : in  std_logic_vector(3 downto 0);
        data : out std_logic_vector(7 downto 0)
    );
end entity rom_16x8;

architecture behavioral of rom_16x8 is
    type rom_array is array (0 to 15) of std_logic_vector(7 downto 0);
    constant ROM_DATA : rom_array := (
        0 => x"00",
        1 => x"01",
        2 => x"04",
        others => x"00"
    );
begin
    data <= ROM_DATA(to_integer(unsigned(addr)));
end architecture behavioral;

to_integer(unsigned(addr)) converts the address bus into a plain integer usable as an array index -- VHDL arrays are indexed by integers (or another discrete type), not directly by std_logic_vector. The x"00" syntax is VHDL′s hexadecimal literal notation, equivalent to 8'h00 in Verilog.

Modeling a RAM

entity ram_16x8 is
    port (
        clk          : in  std_logic;
        write_enable : in  std_logic;
        addr         : in  std_logic_vector(3 downto 0);
        data_in      : in  std_logic_vector(7 downto 0);
        data_out     : out std_logic_vector(7 downto 0)
    );
end entity ram_16x8;

architecture behavioral of ram_16x8 is
    type ram_array is array (0 to 15) of std_logic_vector(7 downto 0);
    signal mem : ram_array := (others => (others => '0'));
begin
    process(clk)
    begin
        if rising_edge(clk) then
            if write_enable = '1' then
                mem(to_integer(unsigned(addr))) <= data_in;
            end if;
        end if;
    end process;

    data_out <= mem(to_integer(unsigned(addr)));   -- combinational read
end architecture behavioral;

This is the same combinational-read, synchronous-write style introduced in the Verilog course′s memory-modeling lesson -- the write happens only on a clock edge with write_enable high, while the read is a plain concurrent assignment that always reflects whatever addr currently points to.

lessons.title: Testbenches & Verification in VHDL
lessons.content:
Advanced

Why testbenches

Just as in the Verilog course, every circuit in this course needs to be checked against its truth table or state diagram before anyone trusts it in real hardware. A VHDL testbench is a separate entity with no ports at all (since it has nothing to connect to outside itself), containing a process that drives the design under test and checks its response.

A simple testbench for the full adder

library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;

entity full_adder_tb is
end entity full_adder_tb;

architecture sim of full_adder_tb is
    signal a, b, cin, sum, cout : std_logic;
begin
    dut : entity work.full_adder
        port map (a => a, b => b, cin => cin, sum => sum, cout => cout);

    process
    begin
        a <= '0'; b <= '0'; cin <= '0'; wait for 10 ns;
        a <= '0'; b <= '1'; cin <= '0'; wait for 10 ns;
        a <= '1'; b <= '1'; cin <= '0'; wait for 10 ns;
        a <= '1'; b <= '1'; cin <= '1'; wait for 10 ns;

        assert false report "Testbench finished" severity note;
        wait;
    end process;
end architecture sim;

wait for 10 ns; advances simulation time, similar to Verilog′s #10 delay, letting the combinational logic settle before the next input change. The final bare wait; (with no condition) pauses the process forever once the test is done, preventing it from looping back to the beginning and re-running.

Self-checking with assert

Rather than requiring a human to read through a waveform or a log, assert lets a testbench check its own results and report a clear failure automatically:

process
begin
    a <= '1'; b <= '1'; cin <= '0'; wait for 10 ns;
    assert (sum = '0' and cout = '1')
        report "Full adder mismatch for a=1,b=1,cin=0"
        severity error;

    wait;
end process;

severity error (as opposed to note or warning) is what most simulators treat as an actual test failure -- typically highlighted in the simulation log and, depending on the simulator′s settings, able to stop the run entirely.

Clock generation for sequential testbenches

signal clk : std_logic := '0';

clk_gen : process
begin
    clk <= '0'; wait for 5 ns;
    clk <= '1'; wait for 5 ns;
end process;

Unlike the combinational testbench above, this process deliberately has no final wait; -- it is meant to loop forever, continuously toggling clk for as long as the simulation runs, generating a free-running 10 ns-period clock exactly like the Verilog course′s always #5 clk = ~clk; pattern.

Writing testbenches like this for every module in this course -- checking each one against the exact truth table, characteristic equation, or state diagram it was designed from in the Digital Logic Design course -- is one of the most valuable habits for catching bugs before a design ever reaches real hardware.

lessons.title: VHDL vs. Verilog
lessons.content:
Two ways to describe the same hardware

VHDL and Verilog both describe digital hardware and both compile down to the same kinds of gates and flip-flops -- the differences are mostly about syntax style, strictness, and heritage.

VHDL vs. Verilog comparison
AspectVHDLVerilog
HeritageBased on Ada, originally a US DoD standardBased on C syntax style
TypingStrongly typed, more verboseWeakly typed, more compact
Case sensitivityCase-insensitiveCase-sensitive
Common industry usePopular in defense/aerospace and some FPGA shopsPopular in commercial ASIC/FPGA design, especially US chip companies
Learning curveMore boilerplate, but catches more mistakes at compile timeFaster to write, easier to make subtle mistakes

Both languages are widely used and most FPGA/ASIC tools support both -- some teams even mix them in the same project. Learning the concepts (entities/modules, signals/wires, processes/always blocks) transfers directly between the two.

Every combinational and sequential circuit built in this course -- adders, muxes, decoders, flip-flops, counters, FSMs, memory, testbenches -- has a matching implementation in the Verilog course, letting you compare both languages′ approach to the exact same problem side by side.

title: Arduino
description: Programming microcontrollers with Arduino C++ to interact with the physical world.

lessons.title: Arduino IDE & Board Setup
lessons.content:
Getting set up

  1. Install the Arduino IDE from the official Arduino website.
  2. Connect your board (e.g. an Arduino Uno) via USB.
  3. In the IDE, select your board under Tools > Board and your USB port under Tools > Port.
  4. Open a sketch (an Arduino program file) and click Upload to compile and flash it to the board.

Sketch structure

Every Arduino sketch has exactly two required functions:

void setup() {
    // Runs once, when the board powers on or resets
    pinMode(LED_BUILTIN, OUTPUT);
}

void loop() {
    // Runs over and over, forever
    digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, HIGH);
    delay(500);
    digitalWrite(LED_BUILTIN, LOW);
    delay(500);
}

This particular sketch is the classic "Blink" example: it turns the onboard LED on and off every half second.

lessons.title: Arduino C++ Basics
lessons.content:
Arduino programs are C++

An Arduino "sketch" is a C++ program with two required functions (setup() and loop()) and access to a large set of built-in functions for talking to pins, timers, and peripherals. Everything else about the C++ language -- variables, types, operators, control flow -- works exactly the same as it does off a microcontroller.

Variables and data types

A variable must be declared with a type before it is used. Common types on Arduino, and how many bytes of memory each one uses on a typical 8-bit board (like the Uno):

Common Arduino data types (on AVR-based boards such as the Uno)
TypeSizeRangeTypical use
bool1 bytetrue / falseFlags, on/off states
byte1 byte0 to 255Raw pin values, small counters
int2 bytes-32,768 to 32,767General-purpose whole numbers
unsigned int2 bytes0 to 65,535Counters that never go negative
long4 bytes≈ ±2.1 billionLarger counters, e.g. milliseconds since startup
float4 bytes≈ ±3.4×10^38 (about 6-7 significant digits)Sensor readings, calculations needing decimals
char1 byte-128 to 127, or one characterSingle characters, small numbers

On 32-bit boards (many newer Arduino-compatible boards), int is often 4 bytes instead of 2 -- always check the specific board′s documentation rather than assuming.

Constants

const int LED_PIN = 13;        // will not change; the compiler enforces this
#define BUZZER_PIN 8            // a preprocessor text substitution, an older style

const is generally preferred over #define in modern code, since it is type-checked and scoped like a normal variable rather than being a blind text substitution performed before compilation even starts.

Operators

Common operators
CategoryOperators
Arithmetic+ - * / % (modulo/remainder)
Comparison== != < > <= >=
Logical&& (and) || (or) ! (not)
Bitwise& (and) | (or) ^ (xor) ~ (not) << (shift left) >> (shift right)
Compound assignment+= -= *= /= ++ --

Bitwise operators come up constantly in embedded code -- for example, reading or setting one bit of a hardware register without disturbing the others.

lessons.title: Control Structures
lessons.content:
Conditional branching

if (temperature > 30) {
    digitalWrite(FAN_PIN, HIGH);
} else if (temperature > 20) {
    digitalWrite(FAN_PIN, LOW);
} else {
    digitalWrite(HEATER_PIN, HIGH);
}

switch statements

A switch is often clearer than a long chain of if/else if when comparing one variable against several fixed values.

switch (mode) {
    case 0:
        // idle
        break;
    case 1:
        // running
        break;
    default:
        // unknown mode
        break;
}

Forgetting break is a classic bug: without it, execution "falls through" into the next case instead of exiting the switch.

for loops

for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    digitalWrite(LED_PIN, HIGH);
    delay(100);
    digitalWrite(LED_PIN, LOW);
    delay(100);
}

This blinks an LED 10 times, spending 2 seconds total inside the loop before continuing to whatever comes next -- an important detail, since delay() blocks the whole program while it runs (the Timers & Non-Blocking Timing lesson later in this course covers how to avoid that).

while and do-while loops

while (digitalRead(BUTTON_PIN) == HIGH) {
    // wait here until the button is pressed
}

A while loop like this is a simple (if blocking) way to wait for an event. do { ... } while (condition); works the same way but always runs its body at least once, checking the condition only after the first pass.

break and continue

break exits a loop (or switch) immediately; continue skips the rest of the current loop iteration and jumps straight to the next one.

lessons.title: Functions & Scope
lessons.content:
Defining a function

int addTwoNumbers(int a, int b) {
    return a + b;
}

void blinkLed(int pin, int times) {
    for (int i = 0; i < times; i++) {
        digitalWrite(pin, HIGH);
        delay(200);
        digitalWrite(pin, LOW);
        delay(200);
    }
}

A function′s return type comes first (void if it returns nothing), followed by its name and a parenthesized parameter list. setup() and loop() are simply two functions that the Arduino core calls automatically -- setup() once at startup, loop() repeatedly forever afterward.

Local vs. global variables and scope

Local vs. global variables
KindDeclaredVisible fromLifetime
LocalInside a function or blockOnly within that function or blockCreated when the block starts, destroyed when it ends
GlobalOutside any function, at the top of the sketchEvery function in the fileExists for the entire time the program runs

Values that must survive between calls to loop() -- like a running counter, or the last time an event happened -- need to be global (or, equivalently, declared static inside the function).

Passing parameters by value vs. by reference

void doubleIt(int x) {
    x = x * 2;            // only changes the local copy
}

void doubleItByReference(int &x) {
    x = x * 2;             // changes the caller's original variable
}

By default, arguments are passed by value -- the function receives its own copy, and changes inside the function do not affect the caller′s variable. Adding & after the type makes the parameter a reference, letting the function modify the caller′s original variable directly -- useful for functions that need to report back more than one result.

lessons.title: Digital & Analog I/O
lessons.content:
Digital I/O

pinMode(7, OUTPUT);
digitalWrite(7, HIGH);   // set pin 7 to 5V (or 3.3V on some boards)

pinMode(2, INPUT);
int value = digitalRead(2);  // reads HIGH or LOW

Analog input

Analog pins (labeled A0-A5 on an Uno) read a continuous voltage and convert it to a number from 0 to 1023 using a 10-bit analog-to-digital converter (ADC).

int sensorValue = analogRead(A0);       // 0 - 1023
float voltage = sensorValue * (5.0 / 1023.0);

Analog-style output (PWM)

Most microcontrollers cannot output a true analog voltage directly, so analogWrite() uses PWM on specific pins (marked with a ~ on the board) to approximate one.

analogWrite(9, 128);  // ~50% duty cycle on PWM-capable pin 9
Arduino Uno pin reference (summary)
PinsTypeNotes
0-13Digital I/OPins marked ~ (e.g. 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11) support PWM
A0-A5Analog inputCan also be used as extra digital I/O pins

lessons.title: PWM & Analog Output
lessons.content:
Why analogWrite() is not really analog

Most Arduino pins cannot output a true, continuously variable voltage -- analogWrite() instead uses Pulse Width Modulation (PWM), rapidly switching the pin fully on and off so the average voltage approximates the value requested.

analogWrite(9, 128);   // roughly 50% duty cycle on a PWM-capable pin

On most AVR-based boards, analogWrite() accepts values from 0 (always off) to 255 (always on), and only works on pins marked with a ~ on the board silkscreen -- those are the pins physically wired to a hardware PWM timer.

Duty cycle and effective voltage

PWM value vs. approximate effective voltage (5 V board)
analogWrite() valueDuty cycleEffective voltage
00%0 V
6425%1.25 V
12850%2.5 V
255100%5 V

This is the same duty-cycle idea covered for DC motor speed control in the Robotics course -- analogWrite() is simply the Arduino API for generating that PWM signal.

PWM frequency

Most Arduino PWM pins switch around 490 Hz or 980 Hz by default (a few specific pins run faster) -- fast enough that an LED′s brightness or a motor′s speed appears smooth to the eye and to mechanical inertia, but potentially audible as a faint whine on some motors or speakers.

Generating a specific tone

tone(BUZZER_PIN, 440, 1000);   // play 440 Hz (concert A) for 1000 ms
noTone(BUZZER_PIN);              // stop immediately

tone() is a separate function from analogWrite() -- rather than a fixed-frequency PWM signal with variable duty cycle, it generates a square wave at whatever frequency is requested, which is what makes it useful for musical notes and beeps rather than dimming or speed control.

Driving a servo motor

Standard hobby servos are controlled with a different kind of pulse entirely: not a duty-cycle percentage, but a pulse of a specific width (typically 1-2 ms) repeated about every 20 ms, where the pulse width -- not the duty cycle -- encodes the desired angle. The Servo library (covered in the next lesson) handles generating this timing automatically:

#include <Servo.h>

Servo myServo;

void setup() {
    myServo.attach(9);
}

void loop() {
    myServo.write(90);   // move to 90 degrees
    delay(1000);
}

lessons.title: Arrays, Strings & Data Structures
lessons.content:
Arrays

int sensorReadings[5];               // an array of 5 ints, initially undefined values
int ledPins[3] = {2, 3, 4};           // an array initialized with values

for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    pinMode(ledPins[i], OUTPUT);
}

Arrays in C++ have a fixed size decided at compile time and are not automatically bounds-checked -- reading or writing past the end of an array silently corrupts whatever memory happens to be next to it, rather than raising an error. Always size loops using the array′s known length (or a named constant) rather than a hard-coded number that might drift out of sync.

char arrays (C-strings) vs. the String class

char array vs. String
Aspectchar arrayString class
StorageFixed-size buffer, chosen up frontGrows and shrinks dynamically on the heap
Ease of useMore manual (needs functions like strcpy, strcat)Convenient operators (+, ==) and methods
Memory riskFixed and predictableRepeated concatenation can fragment the tiny heap on small boards, eventually causing crashes
 
char greeting[] = "hello";           // a C-string: characters plus a hidden trailing '�'
String greeting2 = "hello";           // a String object

On memory-constrained boards like the Uno (2 KB of SRAM total), many experienced Arduino programmers avoid the String class in code that runs for a long time, preferring char arrays specifically to avoid heap fragmentation.

structs: grouping related data

struct SensorReading {
    int pin;
    float value;
    unsigned long timestamp;
};

SensorReading temp = {A0, 23.5, 0};

A struct bundles several related pieces of data into one named type, which is often clearer than tracking several separate parallel arrays (one array of pins, another of values, another of timestamps) that all have to stay in sync by hand.

lessons.title: Libraries & the Arduino Ecosystem
lessons.content:
What a library is

A library is a pre-written, reusable package of functions (and often a class) that handles something so common it would be wasteful to rewrite from scratch -- driving a specific sensor, generating servo pulses, talking over a communication bus, and so on.

#include <Servo.h>   // a library already bundled with the Arduino IDE
#include <DHT.h>       // a third-party library, installed separately

Installing libraries

Ways to add a library
MethodHow
Library ManagerSketch > Include Library > Manage Libraries, then search and install
ZIP installSketch > Include Library > Add .ZIP Library, for libraries downloaded manually
Manual copyPlace the library folder directly inside the sketchbook′s libraries folder

Commonly used built-in libraries

Libraries bundled with the Arduino IDE
LibraryPurpose
Servo.hGenerates the precise pulse timing hobby servos need
Wire.hI2C communication (see the Communication Protocols lesson)
SPI.hSPI communication (see the Communication Protocols lesson)
EEPROM.hReading and writing the microcontroller′s non-volatile EEPROM memory

Classes and objects, briefly

Most libraries expose a class -- Servo, for example -- rather than a plain function. Creating a variable of that type (Servo myServo;) makes an object, and calling methods on it (myServo.attach(9), myServo.write(90)) is how the library is actually used. It is entirely possible to use Arduino productively while treating this as "the syntax the library documentation shows me," without first learning object-oriented programming from scratch.

lessons.title: Communication Protocols
lessons.content:
Talking to other devices

Microcontrollers rarely work alone -- they need to talk to sensors, displays, and other boards. The three most common protocols on Arduino are Serial (UART), I2C, and SPI.

Serial vs. I2C vs. SPI
ProtocolWiresTypical speedDevices per busTypical use
Serial (UART)2 (TX, RX)Up to ~1 Mbps1-to-1USB debugging, GPS modules, Bluetooth modules
I2C2 (SDA, SCL)100 kHz-400 kHz typicalMany (addressed)Sensors, small displays, low-speed peripherals
SPI4 (MOSI, MISO, SCK, CS)Several MHz+Many (one CS pin each)SD cards, fast displays, high-speed sensors

Example: reading an I2C sensor

#include <Wire.h>

void setup() {
    Wire.begin();
    Serial.begin(9600);
}

void loop() {
    Wire.requestFrom(0x68, 1);   // request 1 byte from device at address 0x68
    if (Wire.available()) {
        byte data = Wire.read();
        Serial.println(data);
    }
    delay(100);
}

lessons.title: Interrupts
lessons.content:
Why interrupts

Polling a pin inside loop() only checks it whenever loop() happens to reach that line -- a fast or brief event (a button press, an encoder pulse, an incoming signal edge) can be missed entirely if the rest of loop() is busy doing something else at that moment. An interrupt instead pauses whatever the processor is doing and immediately runs a dedicated function the moment a specified event occurs.

attachInterrupt()

volatile bool buttonPressed = false;

void setup() {
    pinMode(2, INPUT_PULLUP);
    attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(2), onButtonPress, FALLING);
}

void onButtonPress() {
    buttonPressed = true;
}

void loop() {
    if (buttonPressed) {
        buttonPressed = false;
        // handle the button press here, outside the interrupt itself
    }
}

Only certain pins support external interrupts (commonly just two on smaller AVR boards), and the trigger condition -- RISING, FALLING, or CHANGE -- determines which edge of the signal fires the interrupt.

Rules for writing an interrupt service routine (ISR)

  • Keep it as short as possible -- normal program execution, and any other interrupts, are paused while it runs.
  • Never call delay() inside an ISR, and avoid Serial.print() there too.
  • Any variable shared between an ISR and the rest of the program must be declared volatile, so the compiler does not wrongly assume it never changes and optimize away a check of its value.
  • The usual pattern is to have the ISR do the absolute minimum -- typically just setting a flag or a variable -- and let loop() do the real work once it next checks that flag.

Debouncing a mechanical button

A mechanical switch does not transition cleanly -- it "bounces," producing several rapid, spurious transitions over a few milliseconds as the contacts physically settle. Both interrupt-driven and polled button code typically need debouncing: ignoring further changes for a short window (often 10-50 ms) after the first detected transition.

lessons.title: Timers & Non-Blocking Timing
lessons.content:
The problem with delay()

delay() is easy to use but blocks everything -- no other code runs, no pins are read, no other timed events can happen, for the entire duration of the delay. A sketch that needs to blink an LED, read a sensor, and check a button all at their own independent rates cannot do all three with delay() alone.

millis() and the standard non-blocking pattern

millis() returns the number of milliseconds since the board was last reset, and keeps counting in the background regardless of what loop() is doing. Comparing it against a saved timestamp lets a sketch check "has enough time passed yet?" without ever blocking:

unsigned long lastBlinkTime = 0;
const unsigned long blinkInterval = 500;   // ms
bool ledState = false;

void loop() {
    unsigned long now = millis();
    if (now - lastBlinkTime >= blinkInterval) {
        lastBlinkTime = now;
        ledState = !ledState;
        digitalWrite(LED_PIN, ledState);
    }

    // ... other code runs every loop() iteration, completely unaffected ...
}

Using subtraction (now - lastBlinkTime) rather than comparing absolute times directly is a deliberate habit: millis() eventually overflows and wraps back to 0 after about 49.7 days, and unsigned subtraction still produces the correct elapsed time across that wraparound, while comparing absolute timestamps directly would not.

micros() for finer resolution

micros() works the same way but returns microseconds instead of milliseconds, useful for timing that needs finer resolution than a millisecond -- at the cost of overflowing much sooner, after about 70 minutes.

State machines: scaling up the same idea

The same "check the time, act, remember the new timestamp" pattern generalizes into a state machine, where a variable tracks which phase of a multi-step timed sequence the program is currently in (e.g. a traffic light cycling through red, green, and yellow) -- the same concept, and often the same state-diagram design process, as the Finite State Machines lesson in the Digital Logic Design course, just implemented in software with millis() in place of a hardware clock signal.

lessons.title: Reading Sensors
lessons.content:
Digital sensors and pull-up/pull-down resistors

A simple digital sensor (a button, a magnetic door switch, many PIR motion sensors) just needs to present a clean HIGH or LOW to a digital input pin. An unconnected ("floating") digital input reads unpredictably, picking up electrical noise -- a pull-up or pull-down resistor guarantees a known default state when the sensor is not actively driving the pin.

pinMode(BUTTON_PIN, INPUT_PULLUP);   // most AVR boards have this built in -- no external resistor needed

void loop() {
    if (digitalRead(BUTTON_PIN) == LOW) {   // note: pressed reads LOW with a pull-up
        // button is pressed
    }
}

INPUT_PULLUP enables an internal resistor that pulls the pin HIGH by default; wiring a button between the pin and ground then pulls it LOW only while pressed -- which is why the pressed condition reads LOW rather than HIGH with this common wiring style.

Analog sensors

analogRead() reads a voltage between 0 and the board′s reference voltage (5 V or 3.3 V, depending on the board) and returns a number from 0 to 1023 (a 10-bit reading on most AVR boards).

Common analog sensors
SensorWhat it variesTypical wiring
PotentiometerResistance, mechanically, as a knob turnsA simple voltage divider between power and ground, with the wiper going to an analog pin
LDR (light-dependent resistor)Resistance, based on light levelVoltage divider with a fixed resistor
ThermistorResistance, based on temperatureVoltage divider with a fixed resistor

Scaling raw readings with map()

int raw = analogRead(A0);                     // 0-1023
int angle = map(raw, 0, 1023, 0, 180);          // rescale to 0-180 for a servo

map() linearly rescales a value from one range to another -- useful anywhere a raw sensor reading needs to be converted into a more meaningful unit (degrees, percent, millivolts) before being used.

Filtering noisy readings

Raw analog readings are rarely perfectly stable. A simple moving average -- averaging several consecutive readings together -- smooths out noise at the cost of reacting slightly more slowly to real changes:

const int numSamples = 10;
int total = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < numSamples; i++) {
    total += analogRead(A0);
    delay(2);
}
int average = total / numSamples;

lessons.title: Driving Actuators
lessons.content:
Why a microcontroller pin usually cannot drive a motor directly

An Arduino pin can typically supply only about 20-40 mA safely, and the whole board′s regulator has limits too -- nowhere near enough for a DC motor, solenoid, or anything but the smallest LED. Anything that draws significant current needs to be switched by a separate device that the microcontroller merely controls, not powers directly.

LEDs: current limiting

int ledPin = 9;
pinMode(ledPin, OUTPUT);
digitalWrite(ledPin, HIGH);

An LED without a series resistor will draw far more current than it or the driving pin can safely handle. A resistor sized with Ohm′s Law (from the Electricity & Electronics course), using the LED′s forward voltage and a safe target current (often 10-20 mA), protects both the LED and the pin.

Switching higher-current loads: transistors and MOSFETs

A small signal transistor or MOSFET, driven by a digital pin, can switch a much larger current than the pin itself could -- the pin only needs to supply the small base/gate current (or, for a MOSFET, essentially no steady current at all) needed to turn the switch fully on.

digitalWrite(motorControlPin, HIGH);   // turns the transistor/MOSFET fully on,
                                         // which switches the actual motor current

A flyback diode across any motor, relay coil, or solenoid is essential: switching off a suddenly de-energized inductive load (see the Inductors & Inductance lesson in the Electricity & Electronics course) generates a voltage spike that can destroy the switching transistor without one.

DC motors and H-bridges

Controlling a DC motor′s direction, not just its on/off state, needs an H-bridge -- a circuit of four switches described in detail in the Robotics course′s Motor Control lesson. Motor driver modules and ICs (like the L298N or DRV8833) package an H-bridge behind a simple two- or three-pin interface that digitalWrite() and analogWrite() can drive directly.

Servo motors

As covered in the PWM lesson, hobby servos are controlled with the Servo library rather than plain PWM duty cycle:

#include <Servo.h>
Servo armServo;

void setup() {
    armServo.attach(9);
}

void loop() {
    armServo.write(45);   // move to 45 degrees
}

Relays

A relay uses a small electromagnet to physically open or close a separate, electrically isolated switch contact -- useful for controlling AC mains-powered devices (lamps, appliances) from a low-voltage microcontroller pin, since the microcontroller side never directly touches the higher, more dangerous voltage.

lessons.title: EEPROM & Persistent Storage
lessons.content:
Why EEPROM

SRAM (where regular variables live) loses its contents the instant power is removed. EEPROM (Electrically Erasable Programmable Read-Only Memory) is a small block of memory that keeps its contents even with no power at all -- useful for settings, calibration values, or counters that need to survive a reset or power loss.

Reading and writing EEPROM

#include <EEPROM.h>

void setup() {
    EEPROM.write(0, 42);           // write the byte 42 to EEPROM address 0
    byte value = EEPROM.read(0);   // read it back
}

For anything larger than a single byte -- an int, a float, or a whole struct -- the library also provides EEPROM.put() and EEPROM.get(), which handle the multi-byte layout automatically.

EEPROM has a limited lifespan

A typical AVR EEPROM cell is rated for roughly 100,000 write cycles before it becomes unreliable -- reads are unlimited, but repeatedly writing the same address (for example, every single time through loop()) can wear it out surprisingly quickly. EEPROM.update() writes a value only if it is actually different from what is already stored, avoiding wasted write cycles when the value has not changed.

Other options for larger or more frequent storage

Storage options beyond built-in EEPROM
OptionWhen to reach for it
SD card moduleLogging large amounts of data, or data that changes frequently
External I2C/SPI EEPROM or FRAM chipNeed more storage than the built-in EEPROM, or (FRAM) far more write cycles
Flash-based storage (e.g. via a filesystem library)Boards without a traditional EEPROM peripheral

lessons.title: Power Management & Sleep Modes
lessons.content:
Why power matters

A board plugged into a wall adapter can ignore power consumption almost entirely. A battery-powered project cannot: a sensor node that draws a few milliamps continuously might run for days, while the same node put to sleep between readings and waking only briefly can often run for months or years on the same battery.

Where the power goes

Typical current draw by activity (illustrative, board- and code-dependent)
StateTypical current
Actively running, radio/peripherals onTens of milliamps
Actively running, idle CPUSeveral milliamps to tens of milliamps
Deep sleep modeMicroamps or less, depending on the board

Sleep modes

Most microcontrollers support several sleep modes that trade wake-up latency and which peripherals stay active against how little power is drawn. On AVR boards, the avr/sleep.h header provides several modes, from a light "idle" sleep (CPU stopped, timers and interrupts still running) down to "power down" (almost everything stopped, woken only by specific external events like a pin-change interrupt or the watchdog timer).

#include <avr/sleep.h>

void enterSleep() {
    set_sleep_mode(SLEEP_MODE_PWR_DOWN);
    sleep_enable();
    sleep_mode();     // execution pauses here until an interrupt wakes the board
    sleep_disable();
}

The watchdog timer

A watchdog timer can do two different jobs: waking a sleeping board on a schedule (since deep sleep otherwise stops even the normal millis() timer), and acting as a safety net that resets the board automatically if the main program ever hangs and fails to "check in" (reset the watchdog) within an expected interval.

Practical low-power habits

  • Turn off peripherals (sensors, radios, displays) when they are not actively needed, rather than leaving them powered continuously.
  • Sleep between readings instead of polling in a tight loop.
  • Reduce clock speed if the application does not need full processing speed, since power draw generally scales with clock frequency.
  • Choose components (sensors, voltage regulators) rated for low quiescent current when battery life matters.

Serial.print() as a debugging tool

void setup() {
    Serial.begin(9600);
}

void loop() {
    int reading = analogRead(A0);
    Serial.print("Sensor reading: ");
    Serial.println(reading);
    delay(500);
}

Without a debugger attached (which most Arduino setups do not have), printing values to the Serial Monitor is the primary way to see what a sketch is actually doing -- confirm a variable′s value, confirm a function was actually called, or confirm the timing between two events.

Common Arduino bugs

Frequent beginner mistakes
SymptomLikely cause
Whole sketch appears frozen or unresponsiveA blocking delay(), or a while loop waiting on a condition that never becomes true
A variable shared with an interrupt seems to update itself randomly, or a flag set inside an interrupt never seems to be noticedThe variable was not declared volatile
Sketch runs fine briefly, then crashes or behaves erraticallyRunning out of SRAM, often from excessive String concatenation
Digital input reads randomly HIGH and LOW with nothing connectedA floating input pin with no pull-up/pull-down resistor
analogWrite() has no visible effectUsing a pin that does not support PWM (missing the ~ marking)

Checking memory usage

The Arduino IDE reports program storage (Flash) and dynamic memory (SRAM) usage after every compile. An Uno has only 2 KB of SRAM total, shared between global variables, the call stack, and anything the String class or other dynamic allocation needs -- a sketch that is close to that limit is at real risk of unpredictable crashes as available memory shrinks further at runtime.

Code organization habits that scale

  • Give pins and constants meaningful names with const int, rather than scattering unexplained numbers ("magic numbers") through the code.
  • Break repeated logic out into functions instead of copy-pasting the same block repeatedly.
  • Keep loop() non-blocking (see the Timers & Non-Blocking Timing lesson) so the sketch stays responsive as more features are added.
  • Comment the why behind a non-obvious choice, not the what a line already makes clear from its own code.
